title: A Free ManyChat Alternative for Instagram Creators? We Built It Open Source + FREE!
description:
There’s a feature I kept seeing everywhere in creator marketing: “Comment LINK and I’ll DM it to you.”

It’s a genuinely useful workflow. A creator posts a Reel, someone comments a keyword, and they automatically receive a private message with a link, resource, product page, newsletter, or anything else the creator wants to share.

The interesting part is that this simple workflow usually lives inside a paid marketing platform. ManyChat is probably the most recognizable example, but if all you need is Instagram comment-to-DM automation, paying for an entire SaaS platform can feel excessive.

So we wanted to build an alternative that gives developers and creators more control over their automation workflows.

Meet EngagePilot — an Instagram engagement and automation project built to make social media workflows easier to manage.

What does it actually do?

The core workflow is intentionally simple.

You create a campaign and choose a keyword, for example LINK. Someone comments that keyword on an Instagram post or Reel, the integration processes the event, and the person receives a private reply with your configured message and link.

You can also configure a public reply under the comment when supported by the connected Instagram integration.

That means a campaign can look like this:

User comments "LINK" → EngagePilot detects it → Keyword matches → DM is sent

There’s no need to build a complicated funnel for this basic use case.

The goal is simple: make Instagram engagement easier to manage while keeping control of your own project and deployment.

Why build another ManyChat alternative?

Honestly, because we wanted more flexibility.

For creators, agencies, and small businesses, comment-to-DM automation is often used for very specific things: sending a downloadable resource, sharing a product link, collecting interest, distributing a guide, or moving someone from a public comment into a private conversation.

Many hosted platforms make these workflows convenient, but subscription costs and platform limitations can become frustrating as your requirements grow.

We wanted to explore a different approach: building an automation project that developers can inspect, customize, and adapt to their own needs.

The technical goal is to work with Instagram's official APIs rather than relying on scraping or browser automation.

That distinction matters. Integrations should use supported API permissions, respect platform restrictions, and handle authentication and messaging responsibly.

Why open source?

Because developers should be able to understand the tools they use.

An open-source project gives you the opportunity to inspect the implementation, adapt workflows, fix issues, and contribute improvements instead of depending entirely on a closed platform.

With EngagePilot, the intention is to make the codebase accessible to developers who want to experiment with Instagram automation and build on the project.

You can explore the repository, review its implementation, and contribute improvements through GitHub.

Open source also makes collaboration easier. Developers can report bugs, suggest features, and share improvements that benefit the wider community.

Who is this for?

The obvious audience is creators who regularly use Instagram as a distribution channel.

Imagine a few examples:

  • Creators: Someone posts a free guide and asks followers to comment GUIDE to receive it.
  • Developers: Someone shares a useful template and wants to deliver it automatically.
  • Businesses: A brand wants to share product information with interested customers.
  • Agencies: A team wants to streamline repetitive engagement tasks for its clients.
  • Open-source developers: Someone wants to explore APIs, webhooks, background jobs, and automation workflows.

Instead of manually responding to every repetitive comment, a properly configured automation can handle supported interactions and reduce routine work.

The exact capabilities depend on the connected integration, permissions, and the features implemented in the current version.

The bigger idea

The part I find most interesting isn't just Instagram automation. It's how many SaaS products package useful technical workflows into recurring subscriptions.

Sometimes that makes complete sense. Hosting, support, analytics, reliability, and a polished user interface all have real value.

But sometimes developers want something different: access to the underlying implementation, the freedom to customize it, and the ability to run the software in their own environment.

That's the idea behind EngagePilot — making automation more flexible and giving developers a project they can explore and build upon.

Rather than treating every workflow as a black box, we want to make it easier for developers to understand how their tools work and adapt them to their requirements.

Try it

You can explore the project on GitHub:

EngagePilot repository:

https://github.com/AmitDas4321/EngagePilot

If you're looking for an open-source Instagram automation project, a potential ManyChat alternative, or a codebase to experiment with, check out EngagePilot.

Explore the source code, try the project in your own development environment, and see whether it fits your workflow.

If you find a bug, have a feature suggestion, or want to contribute an improvement, feedback and contributions are welcome!

Give EngagePilot a star on GitHub if you find the project useful. ⭐

Let's make automation more accessible to creators, businesses, and developers.`

title: Taking over someone else's PLC program: do these 4 things before you change a single line
description:
You have just been handed a machine that runs — but nobody can explain it. The previous engineer left, the original documentation is gone, or the system was simply "commissioned in a hurry and never cleaned up".

The most natural move is also the most expensive one: open TIA Portal and start editing.

This is the sequence we use when a customer asks us to rescue or diagnose an inherited program. It is deliberately boring, and it exists because the exciting version fails.

Why you cannot start by fixing

In a program that runs, the "obviously redundant" logic is very likely a patch someone added after an incident. You can see the code; you cannot see the incident.

If you change it without a baseline and without evidence, you do not remove the problem — you replace it with a different one. And the new problem is usually harder to find, because you introduced it yourself. Two weeks later you are back at the starting point, now with a second unknown in the system.

The 4 things, in order

① Capture evidence before you touch anything

Archive everything you can currently get:

  • the program uploaded from the PLC, as it is right now
  • the diagnostic buffer
  • the alarm history
  • the actual state of the main I/O points
  • the operator's description of when things go wrong (spoken words are data too)

This is the raw material for every judgement you will make later. Once you start editing, the state of the machine at handover is gone forever. It is the one thing you cannot re-create.

② Establish a version baseline

Save the uploaded program with a dated archive entry and one sentence: "This version was uploaded from the machine on , unmodified."

It feels trivial. It is the only basis on which you will later be able to say what you changed and why — and the only starting point the next person can take over from.

③ Shrink the search space with static analysis and reasoning

Do not guess from the symptom. Run the program through tooling first: division-by-zero risk, array access without bounds checks, block call depth, unused variables, naming inconsistencies. You are not looking for the bug yet — you are trying to convert "one large unknown program" into "four suspicious blocks".

Then list the plausible causes and rank them by likelihood. Resist the urge to work through them in the order they occurred to you.

④ Change only after the root cause is verified

Confirm the root cause in simulation or by single-stepping on site. Then change. Then run a regression pass, because breaking B while fixing A is the normal case, not the exception.

Every change gets the same archive treatment as step ②.

A ratio worth remembering: when taking over an inherited program, about 90% of the time belongs to "understanding what it currently is", and 10% to "making it what I want". Invert that ratio and you will be back at the start in two weeks.

What to ask the other side for

Ask even if the answer is "we don't have it" — a "no" is itself information about how the system has been maintained.

  • A program backup. Any version, the older the better — old versions are what you compare against.
  • PLC model and firmware version (the order number is the accurate one).
  • I/O list or electrical drawings — even a draft.
  • Which faults have occurred historically, and what was done about them.
  • Who knows why a particular piece of logic is written the way it is. That person is worth more than any document.

Scope note (what remote work can and cannot cover)

Program-level investigation — uploading, static analysis, logic review, root-cause reasoning — can be done remotely, and that is how we usually start.

What cannot be done remotely: wiring and hardware replacement, capturing real machine traces, and independent verification of safety functions. Those need hands on the machine.

We publish this because we think the boundary should be stated up front rather than discovered in week three.

This is a cross-post. The original article lives at plc.aiepco.com/en/notes/takeover-checklist/, and our full engineering process is documented at plc.aiepco.com/en/process/.

title: GrassWhisperer 🌿 — A Local AI Outdoor Companion That Works With No Signal
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

I built GrassWhisperer 🌿 — a local-first AI outdoor companion that gets you off the screen and into the world in under 30 seconds.

It's a beautifully designed web app with four AI-powered tools, all running 100% on your laptop with no internet connection, no API keys, and no accounts:

Tool What It Does
🐦 Bird Whisperer Describe what you see or hear on the trail → instant species ID, call sounds, field tips
🌱 Garden Oracle Your city + USDA zone → personalized weekly planting calendar with local frost dates
🥾 Trail Finder Location + available time → seasonal trail picks (fall foliage, wildflowers, sunrise) + gear list
🤔 Ask Nature Free-form outdoor Q&A — foraging, stargazing, animal tracking, gear, safety

Who is it for? Hikers, birders, gardeners, runners, and anyone who wants to feel more connected to the natural world. The app is built around a single principle: the screen time should be the shortest part of the experience. Open it, get your answer, close it, go outside.

Demo

🚀 Run it locally in 3 commands:

ollama pull llama3.2:1b          # one-time model download (~700MB)
git clone https://github.com/PawanTheGod/grasswhisperer
cd grasswhisperer && npm install && npm start
# → open http://localhost:3333

App in action:

The Bird Whisperer tab — describe a bird from the field and get a full identification with call sounds and ID tips:

Type: "small bird, bright yellow belly, black cap, white cheeks, pine tree, making 'chickadee-dee-dee' call"
→ Identifies: Black-capped Chickadee with habitat, call description, and field tips

The Garden Oracle — enter your city and get a planting calendar for this exact week, with frost dates pulled from the model's training data:

Type: "Portland, Oregon, Zone 8b"
→ Get: garlic to plant now, frost date info, soil prep task, and what to wait on until spring

Code

PawanTheGod / grasswhisperer

🌿 Local AI outdoor companion — bird ID, garden planner, trail finder. Powered by Ollama + llama3.2. No cloud, no API keys. Hacktoberfest Touch Grass 2024.

🌿 GrassWhisperer

Hacktoberfest 2024 · Challenge 1: Touch Grass
Local AI outdoor companion — 100% open-source, runs on your laptop, no internet needed.

What It Does

GrassWhisperer is a local-first AI app that helps you get off the screen and into the world:


























Feature Description
🐦 Bird Whisperer
 Describe what you see or hear — get an instant ID with field tips
🌱 Garden Oracle
 Enter your city/zone, get a personalized weekly planting calendar
🥾 Trail Finder
 Find the best hike near you for the season (fall foliage, wildflowers, etc.)
🤔 Ask Nature
 Free-form Q&A — foraging, stargazing, wildlife tracking, gear

Why Open Source Matters Here

This runs entirely on your laptop using Ollama + llama3.2:1b — a tiny open-weight model that fits in under 1GB of RAM.

  • ✅ Works offline on the trail — no cell signal needed
  • ✅ Your data never leaves your device — no API keys…
View on GitHub

📂 Repository: github.com/PawanTheGod/grasswhisperer

Key files:

  • server.js — Express server + all 4 Ollama AI endpoints
  • public/index.html — Full UI with tab navigation
  • public/style.css — Dark forest theme with micro-animations
  • public/app.js — Vanilla JS, zero frameworks
  • setup.js — Auto-setup: checks Ollama, pulls model

Tech Stack:

Runtime  → Ollama (MIT license) — local LLM server
Model    → llama3.2:1b (Meta open weights) — ~700MB, <1GB RAM
Server   → Node.js + Express
Frontend → Vanilla HTML / CSS / JS  (no build step, no bundler)

How I Built It

Architecture 

Browser → Express (localhost:3333) → Ollama API (localhost:11434) → llama3.2:1b
                                              ↑
                                 Runs entirely on your machine.
                                 No packets leave your network.

Open-Source AI Core: Ollama + llama3.2:1b

Ollama is the open-source runtime that makes all of this possible. It manages model downloads, runs a local REST API server (identical interface to OpenAI), and handles inference — all through a dead-simple http://localhost:11434 endpoint.

llama3.2:1b is Meta's smallest open-weight Llama 3 model. At ~700MB and under 1GB RAM it runs comfortably on a 4-year-old laptop. Fast enough for real-time Q&A (5–15 seconds per response on CPU).

Prompt Engineering for Structured Output

The key challenge with compact local models is reliable JSON output. I solved this with tight, schema-pinned system prompts:

// server.js — Bird Whisperer system prompt
const system = `You are a friendly field ornithologist.
Respond in this EXACT JSON format (no markdown):
{
  "name": "Common Name",
  "scientific": "Scientific name",
  "confidence": "high/medium/low",
  "calls": "What its call sounds like",
  "habitat": "Where to find it",
  "funFact": "One surprising fact",
  "look_for": "Key identification tips outdoors"
}`;

Then the server extracts JSON safely using raw.match(/\{[\s\S]*\}/) — handling cases where the model wraps its response in extra prose.

Swapping Models is One Line 

// In server.js — change this to any Ollama model:
const MODEL = 'llama3.2:1b';   // default — tiny, fast, any laptop
const MODEL = 'llama3.2:3b';   // smarter, better JSON reliability
const MODEL = 'mistral';        // excellent at instruction following
const MODEL = 'phi3:mini';      // Microsoft's ultralight model

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A bird ID app that needs the cloud to work doesn't work when you need it most — standing in the woods with no signal watching an unfamiliar bird disappear into the trees.

Here's exactly where open-source AI beat every closed alternative for this use case:

1. 📶 It works offline on the trail.
Once llama3.2:1b is downloaded (one time, 700MB), GrassWhisperer works with zero connectivity. No OpenAI API key. No Gemini quota. No network at all. That's a genuine difference in the real world.

2. 🔒 Your data never leaves your machine.
Where you hike, what birds you're seeing, your garden's location, questions about foraging near your home — none of that touches a server. With closed APIs, every question is logged and potentially used for training. With Ollama + open weights, it stays in RAM and disappears when you close the tab.

3. 💸 It costs nothing to run.
Closed APIs charge per token. Heavy outdoor Q&A use could easily add up to $10–20/month. GrassWhisperer has zero marginal cost after setup — no metering, no billing, no surprises.

4. 🔧 You can swap, extend, or fine-tune the model.
Want a model fine-tuned on bird taxonomy? Swap it in — one line change. Want to add plant identification using a vision model like llava? It's one new endpoint. Closed APIs lock you into their update schedule, their capabilities, and their pricing. Open weights give you full sovereignty.

5. 💻 It runs on cheap hardware.
llama3.2:1b uses under 1GB RAM and responds in under 15 seconds on a CPU. A $35 Raspberry Pi 5 could run this at a community garden, a nature center, or a trail head kiosk. That kind of democratization only happens with open weights.

The screen should be the shortest part of a Touch Grass experience. Open-source AI makes that possible by putting the intelligence on the device in your pocket — not in a data center you're permanently paying to rent access to.

My Agent Session

This project was built collaboratively with an AI coding agent (Antigravity IDE). The agent:

  • Scaffolded the full Express + Ollama integration from scratch
  • Designed the prompt engineering strategy for extracting structured JSON from compact models
  • Built the dark forest-themed CSS with ambient animations and glassmorphism cards
  • Wrote the auto-setup script to detect Ollama status and pull models
  • Built the full frontend — tabs, result rendering, error states, example chips

The entire project went from zero to running in a single session — made possible by the simplicity of the open-source stack. No API key management. No cloud deployment. No billing dashboard. Just npm start and it works.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Ollama / Local Inference: GrassWhisperer is built entirely around Ollama as its open-source inference runtime. Without Ollama, the app doesn't exist — it's not an afterthought, it's the foundation. Every AI feature runs through the local Ollama API with zero cloud dependencies.

title: BirdLens AI: Identify Birds in Your Browser, Then Get Back Outside
description:
BirdLens AI — An Open-Source AI Bird Identification Companion

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass.

What I Built

I built BirdLens AI, a browser-based bird-identification companion for beginner birdwatchers, curious walkers, and anyone who wants to learn more about the wildlife around them.

My approach to “Touch Grass” is simple: use technology to support an outdoor experience, not replace it.

The intended flow is:

Go outside → Notice a bird → Take a photograph → Get a suggested identification → Return to observing.

BirdLens AI lets users:

  • Upload a bird photograph and identify it locally using an open-weight model.
  • Review the top five predictions rather than trusting a single answer.
  • Read sourced information about the suggested species.
  • Save photographs and results in a local discovery journal.
  • Track simple outdoor observation challenges.
  • Revisit saved discoveries and identify photographs offline after the required assets and model have been cached.

The journal turns individual sightings into a personal record of exploration. The challenges give users a reason to notice more of their surroundings.

The goal is to make the screen the shortest part of the experience.

Demo

Live project: Try BirdLens AI

Try It Yourself

  1. Open the app and choose Identify a bird.
  2. Upload a clear photograph of a bird.
  3. Wait for the model to load and run inference.
  4. Review the suggested species, model score, and alternative predictions.
  5. Save the result and explore My discoveries.

The first identification downloads the model. Later identifications can work offline once the production application and model have been successfully cached, provided the browser retains that storage.

New online species references may still need an internet connection.

Please observe birds from a respectful distance. An identification app is not a reason to approach or disturb wildlife.

Code

Public repository: View BirdLens AI on GitHub

Technology Stack

  • React and TypeScript — Interface and application logic
  • Vite — Development and production builds
  • Tailwind CSS — Styling
  • ONNX Runtime Web — Browser-based inference
  • IndexedDB — Local discovery journal
  • Service Worker and Cache Storage — Production offline support

There is no application backend, user account requirement, or paid AI inference API.

How I Built It

An Open-Weight Model Is the Core, Not an Extra Feature

BirdLens AI uses the chriamue/bird-species-classifier, an EfficientNet-B2 model with 525 output classes.

The publisher declares the model MIT-licensed. Its weights are loaded in ONNX format and executed through ONNX Runtime Web.

Without that model and the local inference runtime, the application's main identification feature would not work. Open AI is therefore central to the project.

Running Inference in the Browser

The inference pipeline works as follows:

  1. Decode the uploaded photograph.
  2. Resize and normalize it for the model.
  3. Run the ONNX classifier using WebAssembly inside a worker.
  4. Convert the output into ranked model probabilities.
  5. Display the top five predictions.

Running inference in a worker keeps it separate from the main interface.

Photographs are not sent to a remote AI service for identification. The application does download model assets and may fetch online species references, but image inference happens on the user's device.

Showing Uncertainty Honestly

A model prediction is not a confirmed sighting.

BirdLens AI uses score and prediction-margin heuristics to mark uncertain results as tentative. It also shows alternative candidates so users can compare possibilities.

There are important limitations:

  • The model is a closed-set classifier, not a bird detector.
  • Unsupported species and non-bird images can produce misleading predictions.
  • Poor lighting, small subjects, and similar-looking species can confuse it.
  • Model probabilities are not calibrated identification confidence.

Scientifically important observations should be independently verified.

A Local Journal and Conditional Offline Support

Saved discoveries are stored in IndexedDB, including the photograph and identification results.

In production, a service worker caches application assets. The model is cached after loading, enabling subsequent offline identification.

This is not offline immediately. The application and model must first be loaded and cached. Clearing browser data or storage eviction can remove cached assets and saved discoveries.

Development with an AI Coding Assistant

I used an AI coding assistant to help develop the project. The finished application runs a real open-weight classifier locally rather than using mocked predictions or a hosted AI API.

Deploying on Vercel

Because BirdLens AI runs in the browser, I deployed it on Vercel without building a backend.

My deployment settings are:

Setting Value
Framework preset Vite
Build command npm run model:download && npm run build
Output directory dist
Install command npm ci

The model-download step is essential.

The model weights are ignored by Git. During deployment, npm run model:download retrieves a pinned model revision and verifies its checksum before saving it to public/models/birds.onnx.

The build then includes that model in the deployment so the browser can load it for identification.

No backend environment variables or AI API keys are required.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For BirdLens AI, openness makes privacy, offline use, and model control practical.

A hosted-only AI API would require sending photographs to a remote service and maintaining a connection for each identification. A redistributable model lets the user's browser perform that work locally.

That makes several things possible.

Keep Image Inference on the Device

Users do not need to upload their photographs to a third-party AI service to get a prediction.

Continue Without a Signal After Setup

Once the necessary application assets and model are cached, identification can work without an internet connection.

That is useful for a nature-focused application, where connectivity is not always available.

Avoid Per-Request AI Fees

Local inference does not require paid API calls or credentials. Hosting and initial downloads still consume resources, but each identification does not depend on a billable inference request.

Inspect and Improve the Implementation

Developers can review the labels, preprocessing, model revision, and output handling.

They can also evaluate a different model and adapt the application without depending on a closed provider's inference endpoint.

Open weights do not automatically make a model accurate. What they provide here is control over where inference happens and how the system can be inspected, tested, and changed.

That is the kind of open innovation I wanted to build around: a small tool that helps people understand the world outside without making them dependent on a remote AI service.

My Agent Session

I used an AI coding assistant during development, but I do not currently have a shareable DevRelay recording of the build session.

I am sharing the implementation through the source repository instead.

title: Golden Hours
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

A team project by @shikha_singh_20 and @shreyash_magar.

What I Built

Golden Hour is a calm, mobile-first web app that nudges you to step outside around sunrise and sunset.

You pick sunrise, sunset or both, and how many minutes ahead you want a reminder. When it's time, your phone gets a notification such as "Golden hour in 20 minutes. Take your chai out to the terrace." You go to your balcony or terrace, take one photo of the sky, and enjoy a chai, coffee or snack. Then you tap Done. The check-in is recorded, your streak goes up, and you put the phone away.

It's for people who spend long hours on screens and for people in apartments, where "going outside" can simply mean going to the balcony. The screen is the shortest part of the experience: a short setup, and a tap on Done.

Code

[https://github.com/shikha-code404/golden-hour]

How I Built It

Open-source pieces

  • Gemma (open-weight), run locally through Ollama. We used it to write the reminder messages, treat suggestions and completion lines. We generate them with scripts/make_nudges.js, review them by hand, and save them to data/nudges.json. The server picks lines from that file, so the live app doesn't need a model running.
  • SunCalc calculates sunrise, sunset and golden hour offline from latitude, longitude and date.
  • Node.js and Express for the server, and Web Push with VAPID keys for notifications. The frontend is a plain-JavaScript PWA with a service worker.
  • MongoDB Atlas stores subscribers, reminders and check-ins.

How it works

  1. You allow notifications and share your location. The app stores your timezone too.
  2. A scheduler calls our /api/tick endpoint every minute with a secret header. The endpoint plans upcoming reminders from SunCalc and sends the ones that are due.
  3. Tapping the notification opens an "outside" screen with the camera, a treat picker and a Done button.
  4. Your photo is saved in your phone's IndexedDB and is never uploaded. The server only stores the check-in (date, kind and optional treat) to count your streak.

Data model: subscribers (push endpoint and keys, location, timezone, preferences, lead time), reminders (kind, event time, fire time, sent time) and checkins (kind, local date, optional treat).

Hosting: Render runs the web service, defined in a render.yaml Blueprint with a /health check and secrets entered in the dashboard. Render is only hosting. Any server with Node.js and MongoDB can run the app.

How we built it: We used Antigravity as a coding assistant and built the app in phases (database, sun-time module, API, frontend, messages, deployment), checking each step ourselves.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • We could read and curate every message. Because Gemma is open-weight and ran on our own machine, we generated the messages, deleted the odd ones, and shipped a fixed set. We aren't relying on a hosted model whose wording or terms could change.
  • No per-use AI cost. The model runs once, offline, on a laptop. There are no third-party AI API keys, so the AI part of the app costs nothing to run. (Web Push and MongoDB Atlas still need their normal service credentials.)
  • Privacy by design. Photos of someone's home never leave their phone, and sun times are calculated with an open library instead of sending the person's location to a sun-times API.
  • Swappable and extensible. When a better small model appears, we can regenerate the messages and compare. Anyone can fork the repo, edit data/nudges.json, and add their own language or tone.

Prize Categories

We have used Gemma , Render, MongoDB Atlas for building this project.

title: 🌿 Terra-Gotchi: The 100% Offline AI Companion That Feeds on Real-World Nature
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

Wellness apps usually trap you in a new cycle of screen time. I wanted to build something that forces you to use your phone simply as a viewfinder for the physical world 🏞️.

Meet Terra-Gotchi 🐾—an open-source, fully offline digital pet that survives strictly by "eating" real-world natural textures 🍂. It asks for a craving (e.g., "I want a rough piece of tree bark" 🪵 or "Find me a green leaf" 🍃), and you have to physically go outside, find it, and take a picture 📷. A local multimodal AI acts as a judge ⚖️, verifying your photo before the pet accepts the meal 😋. It is designed for developers, students, and anyone looking to gamify their time away from their desks 🚶‍♀️.

Demo

Code

ShrutiChaudhary08 / Terra-Gotchi

🌱 Terra-Gotchi 🌍

The digital pet that only eats real grass.

A 100% offline, multimodal AI companion that makes you go outside.

📖 Table of Contents

  • ✨ What is Terra-Gotchi?
  • 🎮 How It Works
  • 🚀 Key Features
  • 🧰 Tech Stack
  • 🏗️ Architecture
  • ⚙️ Installation & Setup
  • 🕹️ Usage
  • 🛠️ Troubleshooting
  • 🗺️ Roadmap
  • 🤝 Contributing
  • 👩‍💻 Author

✨ What is Terra-Gotchi?

Virtual pets have always asked the same thing of us: more screen time. Terra-Gotchi flips the script.

Terra-Gotchi is an offline, multimodal AI digital pet built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 "Touch Grass" challenge. You can't feed it by tapping a button. Instead, your pet craves something from the real world:

🗣️ "I'm so hungry... find me a green leaf!" 🗣️ "I want something rough, like tree bark!"

To feed it, you have to put the phone down, walk outside, find the object, and photograph it. A…

View on GitHub

How I Built It

Building secure, local-first systems is a major interest of mine, so I built this specifically to prove that powerful multimodal AI doesn't need cloud infrastructure ☁️🚫. This entire project runs 100% offline on local hardware:

🧠 The Brain (Open-Weight LLM): Google's lightweight gemma:2b running locally via Ollama generates dynamic, creative cravings and reacts joyfully when fed.

👁️ The Eyes (Vision Verification): The llava open-source multimodal model visually inspects the user's camera feed to verify if the photo actually contains the requested natural item.

⚙️ The Engine & Memory: A Python/Flask backend routes the AI logic, paired with an embedded SQLite database 💾 to store the pet's state and interaction history locally.

🖥️ The Interface: A responsive HTML/Vanilla JS frontend utilizes the WebRTC API for live camera capture 🎥 and the Web Speech API 🗣️ so the pet can speak its cravings out loud—meaning you don't even have to look at the screen while hunting for its food.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

The "Touch Grass" theme is about disconnecting 🔌. If I built this using a closed API, the app would instantly break the moment you walked into the woods where there is no Wi-Fi 🌲.

By running gemma:2b and llava locally with Ollama 🦙, Terra-Gotchi becomes a true outdoor companion 🏕️. It costs absolutely nothing to run 💸, keeps all user camera data strictly on their own device 🔒, and proves that we can run complex, multi-agent AI systems in the middle of a forest without relying on a centralized cloud server.

Prize Categories

💎 Best Use of Gemma: For utilizing the open-weight gemma:2b model locally to power the agent's core personality, cravings, and conversational reactions.

title: 5 ways Cancel doesn't actually cancel in C#
description:
A user clicks Export, changes their mind, and clicks Cancel. The spinner goes away. On the server, the export keeps running to the end and saves a file nobody wants.

CancellationToken only works if every piece of code along the way cooperates. Here are five ways it quietly doesn't. Each demo logs a timestamp, the "Cancel" click is simulated, and every output is copied from actually running it on .NET 10. (The demo harness prints Cancelled cleanly when the task ends with a cancellation, and (done) when it runs to completion.)

1. Passing the token to Task.Run and nowhere else 

using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var work = Task.Run(() => BuildReport(), cts.Token);

await Task.Delay(500);
cts.Cancel();                     // user clicks Cancel
Log.Write("Cancel clicked");

await work;

static void BuildReport()
{
    for (var row = 1; row <= Report.Rows; row++)
        Thread.Sleep(300);        // slow work, row by row
    Report.Save(Report.Rows);
}

[0.5s] Cancel clicked
[3.1s] Report saved (10/10 rows)
[3.1s] (done)

Cancelled at half a second, finished anyway at three. The token you give Task.Run is only used to skip the work if it hasn't started yet. Once BuildReport is running, nothing inside it knows about the token.

Fix: pass the token into the work and check it.

var work = Task.Run(() => BuildReport(cts.Token), cts.Token);

static void BuildReport(CancellationToken ct)
{
    for (var row = 1; row <= Report.Rows; row++)
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        Thread.Sleep(300);        // slow work, row by row
    }
    Report.Save(Report.Rows);
}

[0.5s] Cancel clicked
[0.6s] Cancelled cleanly

2. Taking a token and not passing it on 

public static async Task<string> LoadPricesAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    var prices = await Api.FetchAsync("prices");
    return prices;
}

[0.5s] Cancel clicked
[3.0s] Loaded prices
[3.0s] (done)

The method accepts ct, so it looks cancellable. But FetchAsync, like most .NET APIs, takes the token as an optional parameter, so forgetting it compiles without a word.

Fix: forward it.

var prices = await Api.FetchAsync("prices", ct);

[0.5s] Cancel clicked
[0.5s] Cancelled cleanly

There's an analyzer rule for exactly this, CA2016, but in my test it didn't show up in a normal build until I turned it on in .editorconfig:

dotnet_diagnostic.CA2016.severity = warning

3. Stopping quietly instead of loudly 

public static async Task ExportAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    var rows = 0;
    while (rows < Report.Rows)
    {
        if (ct.IsCancellationRequested) break;   // stop quietly
        await Task.Delay(300);
        rows++;
    }
    Report.Save(rows);
}

[1.0s] Cancel clicked
[1.2s] Report saved (4/10 rows)
[1.2s] (done)

It did stop, but break drops straight into the code after the loop, which saves a partial report as if it were finished. And the caller sees a normal successful return, so it can't tell the export was cancelled.

Fix: throw, and give the token to the delay too, so a cancel interrupts the wait instead of finishing it.

while (rows < Report.Rows)
{
    ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();       // stop loudly
    await Task.Delay(300, ct);
    rows++;
}

[1.0s] Cancel clicked
[1.0s] Cancelled cleanly

4. Catching the wrong exception type 

try
{
    await SearchAsync(ct);
}
catch (TaskCanceledException)
{
    Log.Write("Search cancelled");
}

static async Task SearchAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    foreach (var page in Enumerable.Range(1, 10))
    {
        ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        await Pages.LoadAsync(page);
    }
}

[1.0s] Cancel clicked
Unhandled exception. System.OperationCanceledException: The operation was canceled.

Cancellation comes in two exception types. A cancelled Task.Delay (and many async APIs) throws TaskCanceledException. ThrowIfCancellationRequested() throws its base class, OperationCanceledException. Catching the narrower one lets the other crash straight through.

Fix: catch the base class, which covers both.

catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    Log.Write("Search cancelled");
}

[1.0s] Cancel clicked
[1.2s] Search cancelled
[1.2s] (done)

5. A retry loop that retries cancellation 

public static async Task SendWithRetryAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    for (var attempt = 1; attempt <= 5; attempt++)
    {
        try
        {
            await Api.SendAsync(ct);
            return;
        }
        catch (Exception e)
        {
            Log.Write($"Attempt {attempt} failed: {e.Message}");
        }
    }
    Log.Write("ALERT: order could not be sent");
}

[0.1s] Attempt 1 failed: A task was canceled.
[0.1s] Cancel clicked
[0.1s] Attempt 2 failed: A task was canceled.
[0.1s] Attempt 3 failed: A task was canceled.
[0.1s] Attempt 4 failed: A task was canceled.
[0.1s] Attempt 5 failed: A task was canceled.
[0.1s] ALERT: order could not be sent
[0.1s] (done)

The user cancelled, and the code treated it as an outage: five instant "failures" and an alert that pages someone. catch (Exception) catches cancellation too.

Fix: an exception filter, so cancellation passes straight through the retry.

catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException)
{
    Log.Write($"Attempt {attempt} failed: {e.Message}");
}

[0.1s] Cancel clicked
[0.1s] Cancelled cleanly

Recap

  1. The token you give Task.Run only prevents the start. Pass it into the work.
  2. Forward the token to every call that accepts one. Turn on CA2016.
  3. ThrowIfCancellationRequested(), not a quiet break.
  4. Catch OperationCanceledException, not TaskCanceledException.
  5. Retry loops must let cancellation through: when (e is not OperationCanceledException).

Which of these is hiding in your codebase right now? Tell me in the comments.

I make short, tested videos about C# bugs that compile fine and still break things. More on the Naze Code YouTube channel.

Sources: Microsoft Learn, Cancellation in managed threads, Task.Run, CA2016, TaskCanceledException. Tested on .NET SDK 10.0.302.

title: Making LLM ratings auditable: quotes, limitations, and "can't judge" instead of zero
description:
From Auditable LLMs to Auditable Vision Rehab: Why Transparency Wins

A recent dev.to post sparked a necessary conversation about LLM-generated ratings. The author proposed a radical ruleset: fix the evidence window, show the actual quotes, admit limitations, and provide a "can't judge" button instead of inventing a score. The core objective is to stop confident-sounding noise from masquerading as signal. In the world of AI, we call this auditability.

As I read this, I realized that vision rehabilitation for amblyopia (lazy eye) has historically operated in the opposite direction. For decades, the industry has been a "black box." Patients—especially adults who were often told it was too late for them—were subjected to opaque patches, red-blue glasses, and rigid clinic schedules. There was no dashboard, no choice of content, and zero visibility into what the dominant eye was seeing versus the lazy eye. It was a system of "trust the process," which is the medical equivalent of a hallucinating LLM.

This is why the development of Amblyotube by Seven Sports is so compelling from a practitioner's perspective. It applies the same logic of transparency and user-control to the challenge of binocular vision.

The Architecture of Control

Amblyotube, built for the Meta Quest, leverages the hardware's fundamental design—two independent eyepieces—to implement dichoptic vision training. Instead of a static medical device, it functions as a transparent layer over the content the user already enjoys. By using any YouTube video as the primary stimulus, the app removes the friction of "boring" therapy, which is the primary reason teenagers (13+) typically abandon traditional patching.

But the real innovation lies in the auditability of the visual experience. The user is not a passive recipient; they are the operator of their own training session. The system provides several key technical levers:

1. The Dominant Eye Shader: Rather than a binary "on/off" patch, this tool provides digital occlusion. Users can adjust blur, contrast, brightness, and opacity. This allows for a gradual transition from full patching to partial shading, ensuring the dominant eye remains active while the lazy eye is forced to engage.

2. AI-Driven MFBF (Lazy Eye Sharpener): To prevent the lazy eye from simply ignoring the image, the software uses AI-driven processing to identify human figures within the video stream. It then applies a sharpening effect exclusively to the lazy eye's feed. This creates a high-contrast signal that the brain cannot easily ignore.

3. The Magenta Focus Cue: One of the hardest parts of amblyopia is "fusion"—getting the brain to merge two different images into one. Amblyotube solves this with a moving magenta circular cue visible only to the lazy eye (while the dominant eye sees a neutral grey). Magenta was chosen because it rarely occurs in natural video, making it a distinct, high-visibility signal that helps the brain lock onto the target and promote neuroplasticity.

Rendering Pipeline & Latency Budget

Under the hood the app runs a stereoscopic render pass at 72 fps (Quest 2/3 native) with a per‑eye resolution of 1832 × 1920. The YouTube stream is decoded on the GPU via the MediaCodec surface, then split into two textures. A lightweight compute shader applies the dominant‑eye occlusion parameters in < 0.3 ms, while a separate TensorFlow Lite model (MobileNet‑V2, 0.5 M parameters) runs inference at 30 fps to detect human silhouettes for the MFBF sharpening pass. The total frame‑time budget stays under 13 ms, leaving headroom for the compositor and avoiding motion‑to‑photon latency spikes that would break immersion.

On‑Device AI Inference & Privacy

All inference happens on‑device; no video frames leave the headset. The model is quantized to INT8, reducing memory footprint to ~1.2 MB and keeping power draw under 1.5 W. This design choice satisfies both GDPR‑style data‑minimization requirements and the practical need for offline operation — users can train on a plane or in a clinic without Wi‑Fi.

Visual Accents & Adaptive Pulse Controls

To further refine the "lock‑on" capability, the software introduces Visual Accents. These include a yellow‑green glow (Highlight) and a red silhouette (Outline) around human figures. They aren't static; they can be set to a "breathing" rhythm (Hz) via pulse controls. This rhythmic oscillation prevents neural adaptation, keeping the user's attention focused on the target. The pulse frequency is exposed as a slider (0.5–4 Hz) and persisted in the user profile, enabling a simple A/B test: the practitioner can compare session logs at 1 Hz vs. 2 Hz and correlate with stereo‑acuity gains.

Extensibility Hooks

Amblyotube exposes a minimal JSON‑over‑WebSocket API for researchers who want to inject custom stimuli (e.g., synthetic gratings, Vernier targets) or pull per‑frame eye‑tracking telemetry (when the Quest Pro eye‑tracking module is present). The schema is versioned, and the app ships with a sandboxed TypeScript snippet that developers can drop into a React Native wrapper for rapid prototyping.

Engineering Engagement

From an engineering standpoint, this is far superior to traditional anaglyph glasses, which distort the entire color palette of the scene. Amblyotube maintains natural visual colors, making the experience sustainable for the recommended 30 to 40‑minute sessions. The combination of per‑eye shader control, on‑device AI, and a transparent data path turns a historically opaque therapy into an auditable, user‑driven loop — exactly the kind of system we demand from our LLMs.

The Human Result

When we move away from the "black box" and give the user the tools to see—and adjust—their own progress, the psychological barrier to rehabilitation drops. Amblyotube isn't a medical cure or a replacement for professional therapy, but it is a powerful assistive tool for visual coordination and attention. It transforms a chore into a recreational activity.

By treating vision training like an auditable system—where the input is controlled, the stimulus is targeted, and the experience is transparent—we can help more people regain the depth perception and binocular vision they thought they had lost.

Start your coordination practice here: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Developers already delegate whole pipelines to AI. Why doesn't the rest of the business?
description:
I've been writing C# and .NET for 20 years. For most of that time, "automation" meant the build pipeline: push code, tests run, it deploys, and nobody presses a button.

For the last year it's gone further. I've delegated whole pipelines to Claude: not "write me this function", but "here's the job, carry it end to end, and tell me when you need me". Once you've worked like that, going back to prompting an AI one task at a time feels wasteful.

Then I looked at the rest of a business. Support, ops, research, content, bookkeeping. They're pipelines too: work arrives, someone picks it up, does it and passes it on. But they still run on people pushing the buttons, or on AI tools that do one task and then sit waiting for the next prompt.

So I built Jugg.ai to bring that delegated pipeline to every part of a business, not just code.

Hand over a job, a department or a company

You can start small and grow:

  • One team. Give it a standing job, like "triage the support inbox" or "keep a competitor brief current". It works the job, picks up new work as it arrives and remembers what it learned for next time.
  • Several departments. Support, ops, research and content, each with its own team, budget and memory, all working at once.
  • A whole company. Give a CEO agent a mission. It sets up the departments, staffs and funds them from your budget, and keeps them running 24/7. You check in instead of prompting.

It's the same dial at every size: one pipeline, or all of them.

A pipeline that runs itself

The difference from a chatbot is the same as the difference between a build server and running the build by hand:

  • It's triggered by new work. A team watches the tools you connect (GitHub, Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, Notion, Linear, Jira and more) and starts when a new email, ticket or issue lands.
  • It runs without you. It carries the job through to a result rather than stopping after each step.
  • It asks when it should. When it hits a real decision, it brings you that one question instead of guessing or going quiet. Think of it as a required approval in the pipeline.

Memory that lasts, and is shared

Most AI tools forget everything when the chat ends. Here, memory is the point:

  • Long-term memory. Every team keeps a memory that outlives any single job: findings, decisions, what worked and what didn't. When a job finishes, its report goes into that memory and the next job starts from it. Nobody re-explains your product, your customers or last week's decisions.
  • Group memory. The memory is shared by everyone on the team, so what one agent learns, the others can use. That's how a team stays coordinated without you in the middle.
  • It compounds. The longer a team runs, the more it knows about how your business actually works, so week three is better than week one.
  • You stay in charge of it. You can see what a team has remembered and delete anything you don't want kept.

Guardrails, like any good pipeline

You wouldn't run a deploy pipeline without limits, and the same goes here:

  • Hard budget caps for the company, each team and each job. A team that reaches its budget stops; it doesn't send you a surprise bill.
  • A kill switch on every team.
  • Approval before anything risky. By default, agents ask before sending email, inviting people or deleting things. You decide how autonomous each team is.
  • Your own model key. You bring a key from Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI or DeepSeek and pay them directly. I never mark up tokens.
  • Your data stays yours. Each organisation's data is kept separate and credentials are encrypted. Nothing is used to train models.

Honest about the limits

  • If you need one quick answer, a strong chat model is still faster. Jugg.ai is for work that keeps coming back.
  • You need your own model key before you can try it.
  • Google connections show an "unverified app" screen while Google reviews the app.
  • A team of agents is cheap to run, but slower than a single agent.

What I'd love to hear

If you could turn one part of your business into a pipeline that runs itself, which would it be? And would you start with one job, or hand over a whole department?

You can try it at jugg.ai.

title: My weather app says '60% rain' all day. So I made TabPFN tell me which hours to go touch grass.
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Touch Grass

What I Built

In Lagos the weather app on your phone says "60% rain" for the whole day, and then it shines until 4pm and pours at 5. So you either stay in all day, or you go out and get soaked.

Go Out Today? is a morning brief that answers one question: when is the best time today to be outside for the thing I want to do? You pick an activity (walk, run, football, market, drying clothes, commute, picnic, hangout), press one big play button, and a voice tells you something like:

"The best time for a picnic is between 3 pm and 6 pm with at most 29% chance of rain. Outside this window, rain chances peak at 54% around 12 pm."

Then you close the laptop and go. That is the whole idea for "Touch Grass": the screen should be the shortest part. At 05:45 a scheduled job builds the brief, so at 6am it plays straight away.

How it works:

  1. TabPFN looks at three years of hourly Lagos weather and forecasts the rain chance and temperature for each of the next 12 hours.
  2. Code works out the facts: the best window, the window to avoid, any heat.
  3. A local Qwen model through Ollama turns those facts into two or three plain sentences.
  4. ElevenLabs reads it out loud, with captions that light up word by word.

TabPFN and the model run on my laptop: an Intel UHD 620, 16 GB of RAM, no GPU.

It's for anyone who wants to get off the screen and go touch grass today, whether that's a walk, a run, a picnic, a hangout with friends or football with the guys. You don't need to read a weather chart or guess what "60% rain" means. Press play, listen for a few seconds, and it tells you the best time to go out and the time to avoid. Then you close the laptop and go.

I built it for me first. I'm the one who stays in all day because the app said 60%.

Demo

The cold-start part of the video is sped up (it says so on screen). The voice parts are real time, sound on.

The sky follows the real time of day: orange at sunrise, blue in the day, dark with a moon and stars at night. The character on the grass changes with the activity, so dry clothes gets a clothesline and picnic gets a blanket.

Taking it outside

Saturday 10 October. A friend was celebrating his birthday, so I had a party to get to. In the morning I picked Hangout and pressed play:

"The best time to hang out today is from 4 pm to 6 pm, with at most a 29% chance of rain."

It also said there were no windows to avoid, so the rest of the day wasn't a write-off either. I went to the party, and the 4–6 pm window held: no rain. I filmed the brief on my laptop outside, then pressed "I went outside ✓", typed one line and logged it. That log stays in a file on my laptop. It's the only "score" the app keeps: how often I actually went.

Here it is in real use: four activities I filmed on my phone, ending with logging the outing.

One good day isn't proof. Sep 30 (below) was a bad day for it. But on Saturday, it was the reason I left the house in the right two hours instead of guessing.

What my colleague said

Nobody else has used it yet, but I showed it to my colleague at work. She liked the idea of hearing the day before you've even properly got out of bed: you know the forecast and when you can go out, without opening an app.

Then she found the real feature. If you don't feel like going out and Go Out Today? puts the rain right in the window you were planning to go, that's a perfect excuse. I hadn't designed for that, but it's honest: the brief works in both directions.

Code

G00dS0ul-Hackerton / w1-go-out-today

A local, voice-first morning brief that tells people in Lagos the best time today to be outside.

w1-go-out-today

A local, voice-first morning brief that tells people in Lagos the best time today to be outside.

Quick Start

1. Prerequisites

  • Python 3.12 managed with uv
  • Ollama running locally with qwen2.5-coder:7b: 
    ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b

2. Setup

Clone the repository and install dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/G00dS0ul-Hackerton/w1-go-out-today.git
cd w1-go-out-today
uv sync

Copy .env.example to .env and configure your settings:

cp .env.example .env

Key settings:

  • ELEVENLABS_API_KEY: Your ElevenLabs API key (required for audio; or pass --no-voice for text-only).
  • ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID: Voice ID (default: JBFqnCBsd6RMkjVDRZzb - George).
  • ELEVENLABS_MODEL_ID: Model ID (default: eleven_flash_v2_5 - 0.5 credits/char on free tier).
  • TABPFN_TOKEN: Your TabPFN token (required on Windows to prevent browser authentication prompts).
  • OLLAMA_BASE_URL: Ollama API endpoint (default: http://localhost:11434).
  • OLLAMA_MODEL: Chosen Ollama model (default: qwen2.5-coder:7b).

(Note: 3 years of hourly historical Lagos weather data is pre-bundled in data/lagos_weather.csv).

3. Run the Morning Brief (CLI)

Generate a 12-hour…

View on GitHub

Python 3.12 with uv, FastAPI, and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS with no build step. There are 64 tests and they all run offline: TabPFN, Ollama and ElevenLabs are stubbed.

How I Built It

Here's the whole pipeline. Only fetching the latest weather and the voice need the internet.

 05:45 scheduled job (or you press play)
        │
        ▼
 Open-Meteo        last 2 days of Lagos weather + 3-year CSV  (online)
        │
        ▼
 TabPFN            rain chance + temperature, next 12 hours   (local, CPU)
        │
        ▼
 Code: the facts   best window · window to avoid · heat hours (no AI)
        │
        ▼
 Qwen via Ollama   facts → 2-3 plain sentences                (local)
        │
        ▼
 Guard             numbers must match the facts, no "will rain",
        │          no false "at most X%" ── fails twice? → plain template
        ▼
 ElevenLabs        voice + word timings for captions          (online)
        │
        ▼
 Press play, listen, close the laptop, go outside

1. The data: three years of Lagos weather

I pulled hourly weather for Lagos from the Open-Meteo archive (CC BY 4.0): 26,304 rows from 2023-10-01 to 2026-09-30. It has temperature, humidity, dew point, rain, cloud cover, pressure and wind. For real mornings the app also fetches the last couple of days from Open-Meteo's forecast API, because the CSV stops at the end of September.

2. TabPFN: a forecast without training a model

TabPFN is a foundation model for tables. You give it rows, it gives you predictions, and you don't train anything. I used one classifier (will it rain at this hour?) and one regressor (temperature), with "hours ahead" as a feature so a single model covers all 12 hours.

To keep myself honest I held out the last 30 days (forecasts issued at 06:00, 12 hours ahead, 360 rows) and compared against two simple guesses:

  • Climatology: "what is normal for this month and hour"
  • Persistence: "the next hours will be like right now"
Model Temp error (MAE) Rain AUC (higher is better) Rain Brier (lower is better)
TabPFN 0.71 °C 0.733 0.205
Climatology 0.75 °C 0.606 0.231
Persistence 1.61 °C 0.663 0.322
Gradient-boosted trees (same 3,000 rows) 0.69 °C 0.748 0.199
Linear / logistic regression (same rows) 0.85 °C 0.645 0.250

TabPFN beats the simple guesses on every number. Then, the night before posting, I added the test I should have run first: scikit-learn's gradient-boosted trees, default settings, trained on exactly the same 3,000 rows with the same features. The trees edged TabPFN on all three numbers. The gaps are small (0.02 °C, 0.015 AUC, 0.006 Brier) on only 30 mornings, so I'd call it a tie rather than a loss, but it's not the win I was hoping to write.

So why keep TabPFN? I didn't tune anything. No hyperparameters, no training loop: one fit, and it landed within a whisker of a strong tree model on the first go. It also hands me probabilities straight away, and the brief is built on "chance of rain", never "it will rain". With more time I'd backtest more months and try averaging both. TabPFN is not magic, though. An AUC of 0.733 means that when you pick one hour that rained and one that didn't, it gives the rainy hour the higher chance about 73% of the time. That's useful, but it's not a crystal ball.

Two things surprised me:

More data didn't help.

Training rows Temp MAE Rain AUC Rain Brier Time
1,000 0.627 0.685 0.222 28 s
3,000 0.712 0.733 0.205 97 s
5,000 0.691 0.728 0.207 189 s

5,000 rows took twice as long as 3,000 and scored the same. I kept 3,000. I also did not switch to 1,000 for temperature, because that would be tuning on my test set.

More estimators didn't help either. n_estimators=10 gave the same accuracy as 2 (Brier 0.203 vs 0.205, AUC 0.733 both) but took about 8 minutes instead of 3.6. So it's 2 everywhere.

Then I checked one real day. On Sep 30 it called a wet midday (72–81% from 10am to 2pm) that never came, and the only rain fell at 5pm, when it had said 23%. Its temperatures were off by 0.8 °C on average. That one day is why the brief always says "chance of rain" and never "it will rain".

What broke on Windows: my Windows username has an emoji in it (don't ask). That emoji broke how a TabPFN dependency loads OpenBLAS. Then TabPFN's first-run licence login crashed with WinError 10038, because it reads the keyboard in a way that only works on Mac and Linux. The fix was to put a TABPFN_TOKEN in .env and load it before TabPFN starts.

3. Ollama: the code decides, the model only talks

I tested two local models, qwen2.5:7b and qwen2.5-coder:7b, giving each the same real forecast 6 times. I checked every answer with a guard: numbers must come from the forecast, it must say "chance of rain" (never "will rain"), and it must be 2–3 sentences.

  • qwen2.5:7b passed 2 of 6. Most answers were one sentence, and it kept saying "below 32°C", which was just the heat threshold from my prompt.
  • qwen2.5-coder:7b passed 6 of 6.

But "passed" was hiding something. One coder answer said 5–6pm was "the coolest at 26.2°C". 7am was cooler (25.4°C). The number existed in the forecast, so my guard let it through, but the claim was false.

So I changed the design. The code now works out the facts (best window, window to avoid, heat hours) and the model only turns those facts into sentences. The guard checks that every number matches the facts, and that no range claim is wrong ("at most 29%" has to be true for every hour in that window). If the answer fails, it retries once and then falls back to a plain template. The model can still word things badly, but it can't make up the weather.

This is the guard every sentence goes through (trimmed):

def validate_plan_output(text: str, facts: dict) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if "will rain" in text.lower():
        return False, "Forbidden phrase 'will rain' detected."

    sentences = [s for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text.strip()) if s]
    if len(sentences) not in (2, 3):
        return False, f"Sentence count is {len(sentences)}, expected 2 to 3."

    # "at most 29%" can't be stretched to the whole forecast if the peak is higher
    for m in re.finditer(r"at most\s+(?:a\s+)?(\d+)%", text.lower()):
        ...

    # every number in the text must come from the facts the code computed
    valid_nums = extract_fact_numbers(facts)
    for num in re.findall(r"\b\d+(?:\.\d+)?\b", text):
        if float(num) not in valid_nums:
            return False, f"Number '{num}' does not appear in the facts block."

    return True, "Valid"

TabPFN predicts, the code decides, and the LLM talks.

4. ElevenLabs: a voice on the free plan

When I went to claim the Hacktoberfest ElevenLabs credits, the promo pool was empty. So I built for the free plan:

  • eleven_flash_v2_5: about half the credits per character, and fast.
  • Cache by SHA-256(text + voice + model): the same brief is never paid for twice. Files are written to .part first, so a broken download never gets cached.
  • Voice-friendly text: "4 pm", not "16:00", and about 40 words.
  • With-timestamps endpoint: word timings drive the live captions.
  • Every failure becomes one line, and the plan still shows as text.

My first live call used 149 characters. One fun bug: a bad API key came back as a 400, not a 401, and my error message printed every response header to the screen. Now it says "API key is invalid (check .env)" and nothing else.

5. The page: hiding a slow pipeline

On my laptop a cold start takes a few minutes (about 4 in my demo recording), because TabPFN fits two models on the CPU and Ollama has to load 4.7 GB into memory. A spinner for that long would feel broken, so:

  • Pre-build at 04:30 with Windows Task Scheduler, so the brief plays instantly in the morning.
  • The forecast runs once per morning. Switching activity only reruns the plan and the voice.
  • Real progress from the server (Server-Sent Events), one step at a time: reading the sky → TabPFN forecasting → writing your plan → recording.
  • A waveform ring around the play button, drawn on a <canvas> from the Web Audio AnalyserNode and limited to the speech range.

Two bugs I'm glad I caught before recording. First, I picked "Dry clothes" and heard the walk brief, because the cache wasn't keyed by activity and an older request answered late. Now there's a cache per activity, request IDs, and AbortController. Second, the captions came out as Thebesttimeforawalk... because inline-block spans eat spaces.

Working with agents

I built this in Antigravity with a rule that the agent writes a plan, waits for my APPROVE, builds, then stops at "awaiting confirmation". It never marks anything done; only I do. Each milestone has a plan file, a journal entry with the real numbers, and a saved agent session. Most of the good catches above came from me reading the output and pushing back on the plan, not from the first draft.

Things I got wrong first

  • My Windows username has an emoji in it. That broke OpenBLAS loading inside a TabPFN dependency. Don't put emoji in usernames.
  • The captions read Thebesttimeforawalk. inline-block spans ate every space.
  • I asked for Dry clothes and got the walk brief. An older request answered late and the cache wasn't keyed by activity.
  • A model said 5–6 pm was "the coolest at 26.2°C". 7 am was cooler. The number was real, the claim wasn't. That's why the code decides now.
  • A bad ElevenLabs key printed every response header onto the screen. Now it says "API key is invalid (check .env)".
  • I assumed TabPFN would beat trees. It didn't, quite (see the table).

What this is not

  • It's not a weather service. It's one city, one CSV, and a 12-hour forecast from 06:00.
  • An AUC of 0.733 helps you pick your hours. It doesn't promise a dry afternoon.
  • It knows rain and heat, not traffic, flooding or how loud your street gets.
  • The cold start takes minutes on my laptop, which is why the brief is pre-built at 05:45.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • It runs on my laptop. TabPFN and Qwen run locally with no GPU and no cloud bill. Only the voice goes online, and if there's no internet you still get the full forecast and plan as text.
  • My routine stays with me. Where I am, what I do and when I go out never leaves my machine. The only thing sent to ElevenLabs is the two or three sentences of the brief. The "I went outside" log is a local file.
  • I could open it up and change it. I swapped two models and benchmarked them in an afternoon, added a guard, and moved the reasoning out of the model into code. You can't do that with a closed weather API.
  • It's grounded in my city. TabPFN learns from three years of Lagos history in my own CSV, not a global average.

An honest note: TabPFN's code is Apache 2.0, but the 3.5 weights I used are under a non-commercial licence. That's fine for a personal morning brief, and the README links the licence.

My Agent Session

These are the sessions behind the parts of the build where the agent and I had the most back and forth:

TabPFN forecast and the Windows fixes (M3)

W1 M3 - TabPFN rain forecast for Lagos
You

I've identified the issue: tabpfn's browser authentication polling loop attempts to use select.select() on sys.stdin so you can manually paste the token while it runs the callback server. On Windows, select.select() only works on network sockets and will immediately crash with WinError 10038 when passed a standard file descriptor like sys.stdin.

Additionally, I noticed that python-dotenv was installed but load_dotenv() wasn't actually called in the script, so if you had pasted your token in .env, it wasn't being loaded into the environment!

I have created a short-form plan to monkeypatch select.select to safely handle sys.stdin queries on Windows, and to add load_dotenv().
