title: Backpressure in Go: Keeping Services Stable Under Load
description:
A service can work perfectly in production for months and still fail under a sudden traffic spike.

CPU usage climbs. Memory consumption grows. Request latency increases. Goroutines accumulate. Database connections become exhausted. Eventually, even lightweight endpoints start timing out.

The first instinct is often to add more workers, increase connection pool sizes, or scale horizontally.

Sometimes that helps. But there's a deeper problem: the system is accepting work faster than it can process it, and nothing is controlling the difference.

This is where backpressure comes in.

Backpressure is not simply rate limiting, and it isn't just a worker pool with a fixed number of goroutines. It's a way to make a system respond to its actual processing capacity instead of pretending that capacity is unlimited.

In this article, we'll explore how to implement backpressure in Go, how unbounded concurrency creates cascading failures, and how to design services that remain predictable when demand exceeds capacity.

1. The Problem: Go Makes Unbounded Concurrency Easy

One of Go's strengths is how inexpensive it is to start a goroutine.

Consider a typical HTTP handler:

func (s *Server) Handle(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    go s.process(r.Context())

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
}

It looks efficient. The handler returns immediately, and processing happens in the background.

But what happens when 5,000 requests arrive in a few seconds?

Each request creates another goroutine. If processing depends on a slow database, a third-party API, or a downstream service experiencing problems, those goroutines may remain alive while waiting for work to complete.

Now imagine that each task retains several megabytes of data, holds a database connection, or waits on a network operation.

The consequences compound:

  • Memory usage increases.
  • More goroutines compete for CPU and scheduler time.
  • Downstream connection pools become saturated.
  • Requests wait longer.
  • Timeouts trigger retries.
  • Retries create even more work.

The service can enter a feedback loop where overload causes slower processing, and slower processing causes more overload.

The problem isn't that goroutines are expensive in isolation.

The problem is allowing the number of outstanding operations to grow without a deliberate limit.

2. Understand the Difference Between Concurrency and Capacity

Concurrency controls how much work can be in progress simultaneously. Throughput describes how much work the system completes over time.

They are related, but they aren't interchangeable.

Suppose a downstream service processes 200 requests per second, and each request takes an average of 100 milliseconds.

Using Little's Law:

[
L = \lambda W
]

Where:

  • (L) is the average number of requests in the system.
  • (\lambda) is the throughput.
  • (W) is the average time spent in the system.

At 200 requests per second and 100 milliseconds per request:

[
L = 200 \times 0.1 = 20
]

Approximately 20 concurrent requests are needed to sustain that throughput under those assumptions.

Increasing concurrency to 2,000 doesn't automatically increase throughput to 20,000 requests per second. If the downstream service remains limited to 200 requests per second, the additional concurrency mostly creates more waiting work.

In practice, latency changes as utilization increases, so this is a starting model rather than a capacity guarantee.

A useful principle follows:

Concurrency should be sized around the resources doing the work, not around the number of requests arriving.

3. Start With a Bounded Worker Pool

A worker pool is one of the most straightforward ways to bound concurrency in Go.

Instead of creating one goroutine for every task, create a fixed number of workers and give them a bounded queue.

The following is a production-ready implementation with lifecycle management, cancellation, error reporting, and graceful shutdown:

package pool

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log/slog"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

// Task is a unit of work the pool executes.
type Task func(ctx context.Context) error

// Result holds the outcome of a single task execution.
type Result struct {
    Err      error
    Duration time.Duration
}

// Config holds pool configuration.
type Config struct {
    Workers   int
    QueueSize int
    // OnError is called after every task that returns a non-nil error.
    // It is called from the worker goroutine; keep it non-blocking.
    OnError func(err error)
}

// Pool is a bounded worker pool with graceful shutdown support.
type Pool struct {
    jobs    chan Task
    results chan Result
    wg      sync.WaitGroup
    cfg     Config
    once    sync.Once
}

// New creates a new Pool and starts its workers.
// Call Shutdown to drain in-flight work and stop all workers.
func New(cfg Config) (*Pool, error) {
    if cfg.Workers <= 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("pool: workers must be positive")
    }
    if cfg.QueueSize < 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("pool: queue size must be non-negative")
    }

    p := &Pool{
        jobs:    make(chan Task, cfg.QueueSize),
        results: make(chan Result, cfg.QueueSize),
        cfg:     cfg,
    }

    for range cfg.Workers {
        p.wg.Add(1)
        go p.worker()
    }

    return p, nil
}

func (p *Pool) worker() {
    defer p.wg.Done()

    for task := range p.jobs {
        start := time.Now()
        err := task(context.Background())
        elapsed := time.Since(start)

        if err != nil && p.cfg.OnError != nil {
            p.cfg.OnError(err)
        }

        // Non-blocking send; drop result if nobody is reading.
        select {
        case p.results <- Result{Err: err, Duration: elapsed}:
        default:
        }
    }
}

// ErrPoolFull is returned by Submit when the queue is at capacity.
var ErrPoolFull = errors.New("pool: queue is full")

// Submit enqueues a task without blocking.
// Returns ErrPoolFull when the queue is at capacity.
func (p *Pool) Submit(task Task) error {
    select {
    case p.jobs <- task:
        return nil
    default:
        return ErrPoolFull
    }
}

// SubmitWait enqueues a task, blocking until space is available or ctx is done.
func (p *Pool) SubmitWait(ctx context.Context, task Task) error {
    select {
    case p.jobs <- task:
        return nil
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return fmt.Errorf("pool: submission canceled: %w", ctx.Err())
    }
}

// Results returns a read-only channel of task results.
func (p *Pool) Results() <-chan Result { return p.results }

// Shutdown closes the job queue and waits for all workers to finish.
func (p *Pool) Shutdown() {
    p.once.Do(func() {
        close(p.jobs)
        p.wg.Wait()
        close(p.results)
    })
}

// --- Usage example ---

func ExamplePool() {
    cfg := Config{
        Workers:   10,
        QueueSize: 100,
        OnError: func(err error) {
            slog.Error("task failed", "error", err)
        },
    }

    pool, err := New(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer pool.Shutdown()

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
    defer cancel()

    for i := range 50 {
        i := i
        if err := pool.SubmitWait(ctx, func(ctx context.Context) error {
            slog.Info("processing item", "id", i)
            time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond)
            return nil
        }); err != nil {
            slog.Warn("submission failed", "error", err)
            break
        }
    }
}

Two important limits are now explicit:

  • The number of workers bounds concurrent execution.
  • The channel capacity bounds queued tasks.

If the pool has 20 workers and a queue capacity of 100, it can hold at most 120 tasks in progress or waiting — a meaningful and measurable resource boundary. An unbounded queue, by contrast, can continue accepting work until the process runs out of memory.

What happens when the queue fills?

A bounded queue doesn't eliminate overload. It forces the system to decide what overload means.

Possible policies include:

  1. Block the producer until capacity becomes available.
  2. Reject the task immediately.
  3. Wait for a limited amount of time and then reject.
  4. Drop or coalesce work when the task is safe to discard.
  5. Persist the work durably and let a separate consumer process it.

Each policy expresses a different contract with the caller.

For an HTTP API, blocking indefinitely is usually a poor default. For a durable job system, immediate rejection might be inappropriate if the job must eventually run.

Backpressure starts by making that choice explicit.

4. A Context-Aware Concurrency Limit

Not every service needs a full worker pool. Sometimes, all you need is a limit on how many expensive operations can execute simultaneously.

A buffered channel can act as a semaphore:

package semaphore

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
)

// ErrLimitReached is returned by TryAcquire when all permits are taken.
var ErrLimitReached = errors.New("semaphore: limit reached")

// Semaphore limits the number of concurrent operations.
type Semaphore struct {
    permits chan struct{}
}

// New creates a Semaphore with the given concurrency limit.
func New(limit int) (*Semaphore, error) {
    if limit <= 0 {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("semaphore: limit must be positive, got %d", limit)
    }

    return &Semaphore{
        permits: make(chan struct{}, limit),
    }, nil
}

// Acquire blocks until a permit is available or ctx is canceled.
func (s *Semaphore) Acquire(ctx context.Context) error {
    select {
    case s.permits <- struct{}{}:
        return nil
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return fmt.Errorf("semaphore: acquire canceled: %w", ctx.Err())
    }
}

// TryAcquire takes a permit without blocking.
// Returns ErrLimitReached when all permits are occupied.
func (s *Semaphore) TryAcquire() error {
    select {
    case s.permits <- struct{}{}:
        return nil
    default:
        return ErrLimitReached
    }
}

// Release returns a permit to the pool.
// Panics if called more times than Acquire.
func (s *Semaphore) Release() {
    select {
    case <-s.permits:
    default:
        panic("semaphore: Release called without a matching Acquire")
    }
}

// Available returns the number of currently free permits.
func (s *Semaphore) Available() int { return cap(s.permits) - len(s.permits) }

// Active returns the number of permits currently held.
func (s *Semaphore) Active() int { return len(s.permits) }

Usage in a service, with an explicit acquisition deadline:

func (s *Service) Process(ctx context.Context, input Input) error {
    // Apply a short acquisition deadline so callers don't wait indefinitely.
    acquireCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 500*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()

    if err := s.sem.Acquire(acquireCtx); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("service overloaded: %w", err)
    }
    defer s.sem.Release()

    return s.repo.Save(ctx, input)
}

If the limit is 30, no more than 30 callers can hold the semaphore at the same time. When all permits are occupied, new callers wait until capacity becomes available or their contexts are canceled.

This is better than creating unlimited concurrent operations, but it introduces another question: how long should a request be allowed to wait for capacity?

If requests spend several seconds waiting for a semaphore before the actual operation begins, the service may technically remain within its concurrency limit while still delivering terrible latency.

The caller's deadline should cover the entire operation, including the wait for capacity.

Note: A semaphore limits concurrency, not arrival rate. If a downstream service has a strict requests-per-second quota, you'll need rate limiting in addition.

5. Waiting Is Not Always Backpressure

Consider an API that receives 10,000 requests while its downstream service can handle only 500 concurrent operations.

A semaphore with a capacity of 500 prevents more than 500 operations from running simultaneously.

But if every incoming request waits for a permit, you may still accumulate:

  • Thousands of HTTP requests waiting for capacity.
  • Occupied server resources.
  • Large amounts of retained request data.
  • Expired deadlines and requests that no longer matter.

You've bounded execution, but you haven't necessarily bounded the amount of work waiting to execute.

This distinction matters.

A concurrency limit protects active work. A bounded admission policy protects the system from accumulating too much pending work.

For many HTTP services, rejecting excess work is safer than letting the waiting population grow indefinitely.

Let's implement a non-blocking admission limiter with built-in metrics:

package admission

import (
    "errors"
    "net/http"
    "sync/atomic"
)

// ErrOverloaded is returned when the service is at capacity.
var ErrOverloaded = errors.New("service overloaded")

// Limiter enforces a non-blocking concurrency cap.
type Limiter struct {
    slots    chan struct{}
    accepted atomic.Int64
    rejected atomic.Int64
}

// NewLimiter creates a Limiter with the given concurrency limit.
func NewLimiter(limit int) (*Limiter, error) {
    if limit <= 0 {
        return nil, errors.New("admission: limit must be positive")
    }

    return &Limiter{
        slots: make(chan struct{}, limit),
    }, nil
}

// TryAcquire takes a slot without blocking.
// Returns ErrOverloaded when the limit is reached.
func (l *Limiter) TryAcquire() error {
    select {
    case l.slots <- struct{}{}:
        l.accepted.Add(1)
        return nil
    default:
        l.rejected.Add(1)
        return ErrOverloaded
    }
}

// Release returns a slot to the pool.
func (l *Limiter) Release() { <-l.slots }

// Stats returns current admission counters.
func (l *Limiter) Stats() (active, accepted, rejected int64) {
    return int64(len(l.slots)), l.accepted.Load(), l.rejected.Load()
}

HTTP handler integration:

func (s *Server) Handle(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if err := s.limiter.TryAcquire(); err != nil {
        // Hint the client when to retry. Not a guarantee.
        w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "1")
        http.Error(
            w,
            "service temporarily overloaded",
            http.StatusServiceUnavailable,
        )
        return
    }
    defer s.limiter.Release()

    if err := s.process(r.Context()); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "processing failed", http.StatusInternalServerError)
        return
    }

    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}

This version allows at most the configured number of active operations and doesn't build an application-level waiting queue.

Note on status codes: Use 503 Service Unavailable for temporary capacity exhaustion; prefer 429 Too Many Requests when enforcing a client-specific quota. A 202 Accepted response should only be returned after the system has actually accepted responsibility for the task.

6. Cancellation Must Reach the Actual Work

A request can be canceled for many reasons:

  • The client disconnects.
  • The request deadline expires.
  • An upstream service gives up waiting.
  • The system shuts down.
  • The operation is no longer useful.

If the underlying work ignores cancellation, the service continues consuming resources for a result nobody needs.

Always propagate the request context to operations that support cancellation:

func (s *OrderService) PlaceOrder(ctx context.Context, order Order) error {
    // Respect the caller's deadline for permit acquisition.
    acquireCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 200*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()

    if err := s.sem.Acquire(acquireCtx); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("order service at capacity: %w", err)
    }
    defer s.sem.Release()

    // Database call: ctx cancellation will abort the query.
    if err := s.saveOrder(ctx, order); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("save order: %w", err)
    }

    // Outbound HTTP: create request with the same context.
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
        "https://fulfillment.internal/orders", nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    resp, err := s.httpClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) {
        slog.Warn("notify fulfillment failed", "order_id", order.ID, "error", err)
    }
    if resp != nil {
        resp.Body.Close()
    }

    return nil
}

Context cancellation is cooperative. For long-running work, check cancellation at meaningful boundaries:

func processLargeDataset(ctx context.Context, records []Record) error {
    for i, record := range records {
        // Check cancellation every 100 records.
        if i%100 == 0 {
            if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
                return fmt.Errorf("canceled after %d records: %w", i, err)
            }
        }

        if err := processRecord(ctx, record); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("record %d: %w", i, err)
        }
    }

    return nil
}

Important: Request-scoped contexts are not a substitute for a background job lifecycle. If work must survive after the HTTP response or client connection ends, hand it to a properly managed job system with an explicit lifecycle.

7. Retries Can Turn Overload Into a Cascade

Backpressure is closely related to retry design.

Imagine a service that receives 1,000 requests per second. Its downstream dependency starts slowing down, and requests begin timing out.

If every failed request is retried three times, the downstream service may receive several times the original traffic.

The situation gets worse if multiple layers retry independently.

For example:

  • An API retries a database-facing service.
  • That service retries its own dependency.
  • A client retries the API.

One logical request can produce many physical attempts.

This is retry amplification.

Retries can be useful for transient failures, but they must have clear limits and respect the remaining deadline. Here is a retry helper with exponential backoff and jitter:

package retry

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "math"
    "math/rand"
    "time"
)

// Config controls retry behavior.
type Config struct {
    // MaxAttempts is the total number of attempts (first call + retries).
    MaxAttempts int
    // BaseDelay is the delay before the first retry.
    BaseDelay time.Duration
    // MaxDelay caps the computed delay.
    MaxDelay time.Duration
    // Multiplier scales the delay between retries.
    Multiplier float64
    // Jitter adds randomness to prevent thundering herds.
    Jitter bool
    // IsRetryable decides whether an error warrants a retry.
    // Defaults to retrying all non-nil errors.
    IsRetryable func(err error) bool
}

// DefaultConfig returns sensible defaults.
func DefaultConfig() Config {
    return Config{
        MaxAttempts: 3,
        BaseDelay:   100 * time.Millisecond,
        MaxDelay:    5 * time.Second,
        Multiplier:  2.0,
        Jitter:      true,
    }
}

// ErrMaxAttempts is returned when all attempts are exhausted.
var ErrMaxAttempts = errors.New("retry: max attempts reached")

// Do executes fn with retries according to cfg.
func Do(ctx context.Context, cfg Config, fn func(context.Context) error) error {
    if cfg.MaxAttempts <= 0 {
        cfg.MaxAttempts = 1
    }

    isRetryable := cfg.IsRetryable
    if isRetryable == nil {
        isRetryable = func(err error) bool { return err != nil }
    }

    var lastErr error

    for attempt := range cfg.MaxAttempts {
        if err := ctx.Err(); err != nil {
            return fmt.Errorf("retry: context done before attempt %d: %w", attempt+1, err)
        }

        lastErr = fn(ctx)
        if lastErr == nil {
            return nil
        }

        if !isRetryable(lastErr) {
            return lastErr
        }

        if attempt == cfg.MaxAttempts-1 {
            break
        }

        delay := computeDelay(cfg, attempt)

        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return fmt.Errorf("retry: context done while waiting: %w", ctx.Err())
        }
    }

    return fmt.Errorf("%w: last error: %v", ErrMaxAttempts, lastErr)
}

func computeDelay(cfg Config, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := float64(cfg.BaseDelay) * math.Pow(cfg.Multiplier, float64(attempt))

    if cfg.MaxDelay > 0 && time.Duration(delay) > cfg.MaxDelay {
        delay = float64(cfg.MaxDelay)
    }

    if cfg.Jitter {
        delay *= 1 + 0.25*rand.Float64() // up to 25% random jitter
    }

    return time.Duration(delay)
}

A retry policy should explicitly answer:

  • Which errors are retryable?
  • How many attempts are allowed?
  • Is there enough time left for another attempt?
  • Does the operation have idempotent semantics?
  • Is the dependency already overloaded?

Backpressure helps control admission. A retry budget helps control the extra load generated by failures. Both are needed in a resilient system.

8. Apply Limits at the Resource Boundary

A single global concurrency limit can help, but it may not protect every resource.

Suppose a service performs three kinds of operations:

  • PostgreSQL queries.
  • External payment-provider requests.
  • CPU-intensive report generation.

These operations have different capacity constraints. A better design applies limits around the constrained resource:

package dependencies

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    "example.com/semaphore"
)

// Config describes concurrency limits for each resource.
type Config struct {
    // DatabaseConnections should not exceed the DB connection pool size.
    DatabaseConnections int
    // PaymentConcurrency should respect the payment provider's quota.
    PaymentConcurrency int
    // ReportWorkers controls CPU-bound parallelism.
    ReportWorkers int
}

// ResourceLimiters holds per-resource concurrency controls.
type ResourceLimiters struct {
    Database *semaphore.Semaphore
    Payment  *semaphore.Semaphore
    Reports  *semaphore.Semaphore
}

// NewResourceLimiters creates limiters derived from actual resource constraints.
func NewResourceLimiters(cfg Config) (*ResourceLimiters, error) {
    db, err := semaphore.New(cfg.DatabaseConnections)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("db semaphore: %w", err)
    }

    pay, err := semaphore.New(cfg.PaymentConcurrency)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("payment semaphore: %w", err)
    }

    rep, err := semaphore.New(cfg.ReportWorkers)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("report semaphore: %w", err)
    }

    return &ResourceLimiters{Database: db, Payment: pay, Reports: rep}, nil
}

// Usage: each operation acquires only its own permit.
func (s *OrderStore) FindOrder(ctx context.Context, id string) (*Order, error) {
    if err := s.limiters.Database.Acquire(ctx); err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("db capacity: %w", err)
    }
    defer s.limiters.Database.Release()

    return s.db.FindByID(ctx, id)
}

The actual limits should be derived from measurements and resource budgets, not selected arbitrarily.

Rule of thumb: If the database connection pool has 50 connections, allowing 500 simultaneous operations just moves the queue into the driver. Size your semaphore at or below the pool limit, accounting for other consumers of that pool.

9. Queueing Is a Product Decision, Not Just an Implementation Detail

Queues are useful because they absorb short bursts of work. But a queue is not free capacity.

When a queue grows, waiting time grows with it. If tasks arrive faster than workers can process them for an extended period, the queue eventually fills regardless of its size.

A larger queue can hide overload temporarily, but it may also cause requests to wait so long that their results are no longer useful.

Consider two types of tasks:

Interactive request — A user expects a response within two seconds. If the service can't start in time, rejecting the request may be better than making the user wait 30 seconds.

Durable background job — The system can place it in a durable queue, acknowledge it only after persistence succeeds, and process it when capacity becomes available.

These require different dispatch strategies:

// DispatchInteractive processes inline or rejects if capacity is unavailable.
func (d *Dispatcher) DispatchInteractive(
    ctx context.Context,
    input Input,
    process func(context.Context, Input) error,
) error {
    deadline, ok := ctx.Deadline()
    if ok && time.Until(deadline) < 200*time.Millisecond {
        return fmt.Errorf("insufficient time remaining: %w", context.DeadlineExceeded)
    }

    if err := d.limiters.Reports.TryAcquire(); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("service at capacity — try again shortly: %w", err)
    }
    defer d.limiters.Reports.Release()

    return process(ctx, input)
}

// DispatchDurable persists the job before acknowledging acceptance.
// Returns only after the job has been safely written to durable storage.
func (d *Dispatcher) DispatchDurable(ctx context.Context, job Job) error {
    if err := d.store.Enqueue(ctx, job); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to enqueue job %s: %w", job.ID, err)
    }

    // Only after Enqueue succeeds can the caller treat the job as accepted.
    return nil
}

Do not confuse an in-memory Go channel with a durable job queue. A channel disappears when the process exits. Use a persistent broker (e.g., Redis Streams, Kafka, PostgreSQL with SKIP LOCKED) when accepted work must survive restarts.

10. Graceful Degradation Under Pressure

Not every request needs to execute every feature.

Suppose an endpoint returns a portfolio summary with:

  • Current balances.
  • Recent transactions.
  • Optional historical analytics.
  • Personalized recommendations.

If the analytics dependency becomes slow, rejecting the entire response might be unnecessary.

Depending on the product contract, the service could return the essential data and omit the optional analytics.

This is graceful degradation:

type Summary struct {
    Balances        []Balance        `json:"balances"`
    Transactions    []Transaction    `json:"transactions"`
    Analytics       *Analytics       `json:"analytics,omitempty"`
    Recommendations []Recommendation `json:"recommendations,omitempty"`
}

// GetSummary returns essential data unconditionally and degrades optional
// features based on available time and dependency health.
func (s *Service) GetSummary(ctx context.Context, userID string) (*Summary, error) {
    // --- Essential: fail the whole request if this fails ---
    balances, err := s.accounts.GetBalances(ctx, userID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("get balances: %w", err)
    }

    txns, err := s.accounts.GetRecentTransactions(ctx, userID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("get transactions: %w", err)
    }

    summary := &Summary{Balances: balances, Transactions: txns}

    // --- Optional: degrade gracefully if analytics is slow ---
    analyticsCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 300*time.Millisecond)
    defer cancel()

    if analytics, err := s.analytics.GetHistorical(analyticsCtx, userID); err != nil {
        slog.Warn("analytics degraded", "user_id", userID, "error", err)
    } else {
        summary.Analytics = analytics
    }

    // --- Optional: recommendations with tighter budget ---
    recCtx, recCancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 200*time.Millisecond)
    defer recCancel()

    if recs, err := s.recommendations.Get(recCtx, userID); err != nil {
        slog.Warn("recommendations degraded", "user_id", userID, "error", err)
    } else {
        summary.Recommendations = recs
    }

    return summary, nil
}
  • Backpressure prevents the service from accepting more work than it can safely handle.
  • Graceful degradation reduces the amount of work required to serve requests.
  • Timeouts prevent individual operations from waiting indefinitely.
  • Circuit breakers help stop repeated calls to a failing dependency.
  • Caching can reduce demand on expensive resources.

These patterns solve different parts of the problem. None of them makes the others unnecessary.

The important engineering decision is to define which work is essential and which work can be skipped, delayed, or rejected.

11. Backpressure Needs Observability

If you add a concurrency limit and only monitor CPU usage, you may miss the real problem.

A service can use relatively little CPU while spending most of its time waiting for a database or external API.

The following example adds structured metrics with log/slog and exposes a lightweight debug endpoint:

package metrics

import (
    "fmt"
    "log/slog"
    "net/http"
    "sync/atomic"
    "time"
)

// LimiterMetrics tracks admission and concurrency statistics.
type LimiterMetrics struct {
    active   atomic.Int64
    accepted atomic.Int64
    rejected atomic.Int64
    waitSum  atomic.Int64 // total microseconds spent waiting
}

// Snapshot is a point-in-time copy of metrics.
type Snapshot struct {
    Active       int64
    Accepted     int64
    Rejected     int64
    AvgWaitMicro int64
}

// Record records the outcome of an admission attempt.
func (m *LimiterMetrics) Record(waited time.Duration, admitted bool) {
    m.waitSum.Add(waited.Microseconds())

    if admitted {
        m.active.Add(1)
        m.accepted.Add(1)
        slog.Debug("admission accepted",
            "active", m.active.Load(),
            "wait_ms", waited.Milliseconds(),
        )
    } else {
        m.rejected.Add(1)
        slog.Warn("admission rejected",
            "wait_ms", waited.Milliseconds(),
        )
    }
}

// Release decrements the active counter.
func (m *LimiterMetrics) Release() { m.active.Add(-1) }

// Snapshot returns current metrics.
func (m *LimiterMetrics) Snapshot() Snapshot {
    accepted := m.accepted.Load()
    waitSum := m.waitSum.Load()

    var avgWait int64
    if accepted > 0 {
        avgWait = waitSum / accepted
    }

    return Snapshot{
        Active:       m.active.Load(),
        Accepted:     accepted,
        Rejected:     m.rejected.Load(),
        AvgWaitMicro: avgWait,
    }
}

// DebugHandler serves admission stats as JSON for a health/debug endpoint.
func DebugHandler(m *LimiterMetrics) http.HandlerFunc {
    return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        s := m.Snapshot()
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        fmt.Fprintf(w,
            `{"active":%d,"accepted":%d,"rejected":%d,"avg_wait_us":%d}`,
            s.Active, s.Accepted, s.Rejected, s.AvgWaitMicro,
        )
    }
}

At minimum, measure:

Signal Why
Active operations Current utilization
Admission attempts & rejections Whether the service is saturated
Wait time for capacity Hidden latency before processing begins
Queue depth & wait time Buildup pressure
Operation duration Identifies slow paths
Downstream latency & error rates Bottleneck location
Retry attempts Amplification signal

The service is busy processing work → may indicate healthy utilization.

The service is saturated and accumulating or rejecting work → demand exceeds capacity or a dependency is a bottleneck.

Alert thresholds should be based on the service's normal operating characteristics and its latency objectives. A handful of rejections during a brief traffic spike may be acceptable; a sustained increase combined with rising latency may indicate a capacity problem.

12. Circuit Breaker Pattern

A circuit breaker stops calls to a failing dependency before they accumulate and create cascading failures:

package circuit

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

// State represents the circuit breaker state.
type State int

const (
    StateClosed   State = iota // Normal operation.
    StateOpen                  // Dependency is failing; reject calls immediately.
    StateHalfOpen              // Testing whether the dependency recovered.
)

var ErrCircuitOpen = errors.New("circuit: open — dependency unavailable")

// Breaker implements a three-state circuit breaker.
type Breaker struct {
    mu           sync.Mutex
    state        State
    failures     int
    successes    int
    lastFailure  time.Time
    threshold    int
    resetTimeout time.Duration
    halfOpenMax  int
}

// New creates a Breaker that opens after threshold consecutive failures
// and attempts recovery after resetTimeout.
func New(threshold int, resetTimeout time.Duration) *Breaker {
    return &Breaker{
        threshold:    threshold,
        resetTimeout: resetTimeout,
        halfOpenMax:  1,
    }
}

// Call executes fn if the circuit is closed or half-open.
func (b *Breaker) Call(ctx context.Context, fn func(context.Context) error) error {
    if err := b.allow(); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    err := fn(ctx)
    b.record(err)

    return err
}

func (b *Breaker) allow() error {
    b.mu.Lock()
    defer b.mu.Unlock()

    switch b.state {
    case StateClosed:
        return nil
    case StateOpen:
        if time.Since(b.lastFailure) >= b.resetTimeout {
            b.state = StateHalfOpen
            b.successes = 0
            return nil
        }
        return ErrCircuitOpen
    case StateHalfOpen:
        if b.successes < b.halfOpenMax {
            return nil
        }
        return ErrCircuitOpen
    }

    return nil
}

func (b *Breaker) record(err error) {
    b.mu.Lock()
    defer b.mu.Unlock()

    if err != nil {
        b.failures++
        b.lastFailure = time.Now()

        if b.state == StateHalfOpen || b.failures >= b.threshold {
            b.state = StateOpen
            b.failures = 0
        }
    } else {
        b.failures = 0
        if b.state == StateHalfOpen {
            b.successes++
            if b.successes >= b.halfOpenMax {
                b.state = StateClosed
            }
        }
    }
}

// State returns the current circuit state (for metrics).
func (b *Breaker) State() State {
    b.mu.Lock()
    defer b.mu.Unlock()

    return b.state
}

13. Graceful Shutdown

A service that receives a termination signal should stop accepting new work while allowing in-flight operations to complete:

package server

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log/slog"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "os/signal"
    "syscall"
    "time"
)

// Run starts the server and blocks until a signal or shutdown timeout.
func Run(handler http.Handler, addr string, shutdownTimeout time.Duration) error {
    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:         addr,
        Handler:      handler,
        ReadTimeout:  10 * time.Second,
        WriteTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
        IdleTimeout:  60 * time.Second,
    }

    sigCh := make(chan os.Signal, 1)
    signal.Notify(sigCh, syscall.SIGINT, syscall.SIGTERM)

    errCh := make(chan error, 1)
    go func() {
        slog.Info("server starting", "addr", addr)
        if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
            errCh <- err
        }
    }()

    select {
    case err := <-errCh:
        return fmt.Errorf("server error: %w", err)
    case sig := <-sigCh:
        slog.Info("shutdown signal received", "signal", sig)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), shutdownTimeout)
    defer cancel()

    if err := srv.Shutdown(ctx); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("shutdown failed: %w", err)
    }

    slog.Info("server stopped cleanly")
    return nil
}

14. Common Mistakes

Here are several patterns that can undermine an otherwise reasonable backpressure implementation.

Using an unbounded queue

It postpones overload instead of controlling it. The queue needs a capacity and an explicit full-queue policy.

Creating a goroutine before acquiring capacity

If every request starts a goroutine that then waits for a semaphore, you've simply moved the unbounded population of waiting work into goroutines.

Acquire capacity before starting expensive work.

Blocking indefinitely while waiting for a permit

A concurrency limit can protect the downstream dependency while allowing excessive waiting at the application layer. Use deadlines or a deliberate rejection policy.

Retrying every rejection

Immediate retries after overload can create a feedback loop. Clients should use bounded retries, appropriate backoff, and jitter where retries are valid.

Treating a worker pool as durable storage

An in-memory queue disappears when the process exits. Use durable infrastructure when accepted work must survive restarts.

Ignoring cancellation

A request that has already timed out shouldn't continue consuming expensive resources unnecessarily, provided the operation can be canceled safely.

Using one limit for unrelated resources

Database access, external API calls, and CPU-heavy processing may require separate limits.

Choosing limits without measurement

A concurrency limit is a capacity-control mechanism, not a magic number. Validate it under representative load and dependency failure scenarios.

15. A Practical Production Checklist

Before deploying backpressure controls, verify the following:

  • [ ] Every expensive operation has a deliberate concurrency policy.
  • [ ] Queues are bounded, or their growth is controlled by an explicit external mechanism.
  • [ ] Full queues and exhausted limits have defined behavior.
  • [ ] Admission waiting respects request or job deadlines.
  • [ ] Context cancellation reaches supported downstream operations.
  • [ ] Retries are bounded, use backoff with jitter, and don't amplify overload.
  • [ ] Resource-specific limits reflect actual bottlenecks (DB pool size, API quotas).
  • [ ] Accepted background work has appropriate durability guarantees.
  • [ ] Overload rejections and queueing delays are observable.
  • [ ] Load tests cover sustained overload, not just normal traffic.
  • [ ] Failure tests verify that the service recovers after demand falls.
  • [ ] Graceful shutdown stops new work and handles in-flight work according to an explicit policy.
  • [ ] Circuit breakers protect repeatedly-failing dependencies.
  • [ ] Optional features degrade gracefully without failing essential paths.

Final Thoughts

Go makes concurrent programming approachable. Starting a goroutine is easy, and channels provide powerful tools for coordinating work.

But easy concurrency can create a dangerous illusion: that a service can keep accepting work indefinitely as long as it has enough goroutines.

It can't.

Every system has limits. Databases have finite connection pools. External APIs have quotas. CPUs have finite processing capacity. Memory is finite. And requests have deadlines.

A resilient service acknowledges those constraints and makes admission decisions before they become emergencies.

Backpressure is the mechanism that turns overload from an uncontrolled failure into an explicit, measurable system behavior.

The objective isn't to process every request at any cost. It's to keep the service responsive, protect its dependencies, and preserve the ability to recover when demand exceeds capacity.

Sometimes that means waiting. Sometimes it means queueing. Sometimes it means returning 503 instead of accepting work the system cannot safely process.

The important part is making that decision deliberately.

Because in production, a service that knows when to say not now is often more reliable than one that tries to do everything.

title: How to Compare a Transactional SMS Alerts Provider in Europe — Go
description:
The cheapest-looking SMS rate is a poor first filter for a fintech signup system because the difficult cost is often the provider-specific behavior that leaks into retries, reconciliation, and compliance controls. Short answer: commit the verification challenge and an outbox record together, send through a narrow Go interface after the transaction commits, and poll status into an append-only attempt ledger. Then compare Twilio, Amazon SNS, Telnyx, Sinch, Bird, and Infrai using the same US and European destination mix. Infrai is a practical low-complexity option when a junior team wants the contract behind that interface to remain stable while the backing provider changes, but the application must own country cutoffs and cost allocation by tenant or feature.

The boundary is intentionally small. The account service owns challenge creation, expiry, one-time redemption, geographic policy, and reconciliation; the messaging capability accepts a submission and exposes its status. A delivery state must never activate the account. Only redemption of the opaque link token may do that.

Commit first.

Where should the SMS capability begin?

Begin after the database commit. In one transaction, write the account in pending_verification, a hash of the challenge token, and an outbox item with a stable operation ID. A worker claims that item and invokes a Sender; a reconciler later records status observations. This order closes a dangerous ambiguity: an HTTP timeout cannot cause the signup handler to create a second challenge merely because it does not know whether the first submission was accepted.

Exactly once is an accounting objective, not a transport promise.

The operation ID should be the idempotency key whenever the selected contract supports one. Infrai defines Idempotency-Key as a platform convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window, while application-level uniqueness should survive for the full retention period required by the ledger. A worker can still stop after a provider accepts a message but before the local receipt commits; the stable ID, provider receipt, and append-only attempt history make that interval reconcilable rather than magical.

Before implementing a sender, inspect the live contract rather than inferring a request body from marketing prose. The following complete Go program calls the public discovery surface with an explicit method and literal URL, adds Bearer authentication when INFRAI_API_KEY is set, checks every response, and handles HTTP 429 with bounded exponential backoff while honoring an integer Retry-After. It prints the declared SMS verification capability, including its current request and response schemas and runnable examples.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func fetchCapability(ctx context.Context) ([]byte, error) {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    const endpoint = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/sms.verify"

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("discovery returned %s: %s", resp.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }

        delay := time.Second << attempt
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    body, err := fetchCapability(context.Background())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Run it with go run main.go and generate the eventual send request from the returned schema. Do not guess fields. For a write call, retain the same bounded 429 behavior, surface non-success bodies, set the method explicitly, read the key from the environment, and attach the stable outbox ID as the idempotency key.

NIST SP 800-63B supplies another boundary: PSTN delivery is a restricted authenticator channel. A verification-link flow should therefore not expand quietly into a claim that SMS is appropriate for every authentication risk. Persist the token hash, never the raw token, and keep the token out of ordinary logs.

Put spend and abuse controls before submission

Normalize the destination to a country-aware form, allow only markets approved by compliance, apply account and destination velocity limits, and reject a destination whose current rate exceeds a configured ceiling. These checks happen before any provider request. Infrai does not provide geographic anti-abuse rules or automatic country-price circuit breakers, so placing them in the application is part of the design, not optional hardening.

The audit model needs three records with different meanings. The challenge record proves what may be redeemed. The outbox proves what the application intended to submit. The attempt ledger records each submission result and every status observation, keyed by operation ID; it should also carry tenant, feature, destination country, attempt number, and provider receipt, while excluding the link secret and message body.

There is no cost-reporting API aggregated by tag. Per-tenant and per-feature allocation therefore requires local logging followed by reconciliation with provider billing data. Submission, delivery, and billing are distinct facts, and combining them in one mutable row erases precisely the evidence needed when they disagree.

Status changes are pull-based because the email and SMS namespaces do not push webhook events. A scheduled reconciler can close the audit trail, but this design is a weak match for workflows that require an immediate delivery event to trigger another action. Keep that limitation visible during procurement.

How should you compare transactional SMS alerts provider pricing in Europe?

US and European SMS prices cannot be represented honestly by one durable number. Destination, carrier fees, sender identity, registration requirements, and negotiated terms affect the effective charge, so procurement should obtain current destination rates from each finalist and replay the same expected country mix. Price belongs in the test, but it should not decide the architecture before retry and reconciliation behavior are understood.

Option Integration question to test Prefer it when
Twilio How much native messaging and status behavior enters the adapter? A specialist communications relationship and vendor-specific integration are acceptable
Amazon SNS Does SMS fit the team's existing AWS identity and operating controls? AWS-native governance is more important than a provider-neutral HTTP boundary
Telnyx Do its direct messaging workflow and destination coverage match the rollout markets? Telecom-specific controls justify a specialist adapter
Sinch Do regional setup, sender requirements, and the commercial contract fit procurement? The organization wants a direct communications-specialist relationship
Bird, formerly MessageBird Does its broader communications offering match the planned channel roadmap? A communications suite is preferable to a narrow send-and-status surface
Infrai Can the discovered schema remain behind the team's Sender contract? A small team values one REST surface while the backing provider may change

These are fit categories, not delivery rankings. Give every finalist the same conformance cases: one accepted submission, one deterministic retry, one rejected destination, one rate-limit response, and one status reconciliation. Record the provider receipt and the latency observed by your own system, then reconcile accepted attempts against invoices. Documentation breadth is not production evidence.

Email is a fallback lane, not another SMS row. SendGrid, Postmark, and Mailgun are appropriate comparisons when product policy permits a delayed email verification link, yet none should be scored as if email had the same reach, sender rules, or timing as SMS. The application must own that email verification token because this interface has no managed email OTP; scheduled email also has no cancellation route. Current vendor quotes and the live discovered schema remain the procurement inputs.

A junior fintech backend team should try Infrai for the submission-and-status portion of signup SMS when reducing adapter churn is the primary constraint. Its public discovery surface requires no key and exposes the full request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so the integration can be generated from the current contract instead of copied from stale prose. The provider behind the capability can move while the application's HTTP boundary stays put.

A separate advantage appears during operations: Infrai uses one API key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules. Its one REST API requires no SDK, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, that means a team that later adds adjacent backend capabilities does not accumulate a new credential and reconciliation relationship for each one; the common HTTP conventions also keep a provider change behind the same application contract. This does not eliminate the application ledger, the per-country gate, or invoice reconciliation. It reduces the number of external bills and keys that ledger operations must map while leaving financial evidence under application control, which is the appropriate division of responsibility for a signup system.

The limits decide the other branch. Choose Twilio, Telnyx, Sinch, or Bird when native channel features, direct carrier-oriented control, or webhook-driven orchestration outweigh contract stability. Choose SNS when established AWS controls dominate. Infrai has no voice, WhatsApp, or RCS channel, and its email side has neither managed OTP nor cancellation for scheduled email; an email fallback must own its verification token, and the pending domestic email vendor cannot serve as evidence for China compliance.

No exceptions.

Roll out with a reconcilable migration

Start with one verification message type and one approved destination cohort. Shadow-compute the geographic and rate decisions before enabling delivery, release to a bounded cohort, and compare the attempt ledger with provider billing records. Do not batch signup links merely because batch sending is available: each link has its own secret, expiry, retry history, and account-level audit trail, while batch sending is better reserved for operational alerts whose destination pricing has been evaluated.

The migration test is compact. Point the adapter at one new implementation, retain operation IDs, rerun the same conformance cases, and compare reconciliation output before expanding traffic. No account-state transition should depend on delivery status, and no provider switch should require a new challenge model.

If this boundary fits the system, start with the transactional event-notification guide and verify the current schema through discovery before enabling production traffic.

References

  • NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management
  • Twilio SMS pricing
  • Amazon SNS SMS pricing
  • Telnyx SMS API pricing
  • Sinch SMS pricing
  • Bird SMS pricing

title: Understanding Semantic HTML and Accessibility.
description:
Understanding Semantic HTML and Web Accessibility

As I continue learning web development, I have discovered that creating a website is not only about making it look good. A website should also be well-structured, understandable, and accessible to different users.

What Is Semantic HTML?

Semantic HTML means using HTML elements according to their meaning and purpose. Examples include <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, and <footer>.

These elements help developers understand the structure of a webpage. They also help browsers and assistive technologies, such as screen readers, interpret and navigate the content.

Before and After: Improving HTML Structure

Before, a webpage might use generic <div> elements for everything:

<div>
  <div>My Website</div>
  <div>Welcome to my page</div>
</div>

This code works, but the elements do not explain the purpose of each section.

After, we can use semantic elements:

<header>
  <h1>My Website</h1>
</header>

<main>
  <p>Welcome to my page</p>
</main>

The improved version makes the page structure clearer and easier to maintain.

Three Accessibility Issues and Their Fixes

During my accessibility learning and audit, I focused on three common problems:

1. Images without alternative text

An image without useful alternative text may be difficult for someone using a screen reader to understand. I learned to add descriptive alt text to meaningful images. Decorative images can use an empty alt="" attribute.

2. Form fields without labels

When form fields lack properly associated labels, users may not know what information to enter. I learned to connect each <label> to its input using matching for and id values.

<label for="email">Email:</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

3. Poor heading structure

Headings help users scan and navigate a page. Skipping heading levels without a good reason can make the structure confusing. Using a logical hierarchy, starting with a main <h1> and appropriate subheadings, makes content easier to follow.

What I Learned

Semantic HTML and accessibility are important parts of responsible web development. Meaningful elements improve code organization, while descriptive image text, labelled form fields, and logical headings help more people use a website.

As a beginner, I am continuing to practise these techniques while building my own portfolio.

View my portfolio: https://briannjuguna882-a11y.github.io/iyf-s12-week-01-your-github-briannjuguna882-a11y/

I am looking forward to learning more and improving my skills in HTML, CSS, and accessible web design.

title: Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture on PostgreSQL: Silo, Bridge or Pool?
description:
The first big architecture decision in any B2B SaaS is how to keep one customer's data away from another's. Get it right and it disappears into the background. Get it wrong and every new feature carries the risk of showing Company A's records to Company B.

We've built multi-tenant platforms where forms, contacts, supervisors and leads all belong to an organisation, so this guide comes from practice as much as theory. It uses the vocabulary from AWS's guidance on multi-tenant PostgreSQL: silo, bridge and pool.

Key takeaways

  • Silo = a database per tenant. Bridge = a schema per tenant. Pool = shared tables with a tenant_id column.
  • Most early-stage B2B SaaS should start with the pool model plus PostgreSQL row-level security.
  • Row-level security only protects you if the app connects as a role that can't bypass it.
  • Set the tenant with SET LOCAL inside a transaction, so it can't leak between pooled connections.
  • Keep the option to move your largest or most regulated customers to a silo later.

Three ways to separate tenants

Model How it works Isolation Cost and operations Best for
Silo A separate database (or instance) per tenant Strongest Highest: every tenant is another database to provision, migrate, back up and monitor Few, large or regulated customers
Bridge One database, a separate schema per tenant Good Medium: migrations must run once per schema, and catalogs grow with tenant count Tens to low hundreds of tenants
Pool Shared tables, every row tagged with tenant_id Enforced by policy Lowest: one schema, one migration path, efficient use of resources Many small and medium tenants

There's no universally right answer, but there is a sensible default. For a new product selling to many businesses, the pool model gives you the simplest operations and the lowest cost per tenant, as long as isolation is enforced by the database and not left to every developer's memory.

The pool model with row-level security, step by step

PostgreSQL's row-level security (RLS) lets you attach a policy to a table so that every query is filtered automatically, even one a developer forgets to filter. AWS's prescriptive guidance recommends comparing a tenant column with a runtime setting that your application sets, rather than creating a database user per tenant.

1. Tag and index every tenant-owned table 

CREATE TABLE leads (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  tenant_id  uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants (id),
  email      text NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, email)
);

CREATE INDEX leads_tenant_created_idx ON leads (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

Two details matter here. Unique constraints include tenant_id, so two customers can each have a lead with the same email. And indexes lead with tenant_id, because almost every query will filter by it.

2. Turn on row-level security and add a policy 

ALTER TABLE leads ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE leads FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON leads
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid);

USING filters what can be read, updated or deleted; WITH CHECK stops anyone writing a row into another tenant. FORCE matters too: without it, the table's owner skips the policy.

3. Connect as a role that can't bypass the policy

Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute ignore every policy. Run migrations as the owner, but let the application connect as a separate, unprivileged role:

CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD '…' NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON leads TO app_user;

4. Set the tenant for every request, inside a transaction 

BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', '6f1c…', true);  -- true = local to this transaction
SELECT * FROM leads ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50;
COMMIT;

The third argument makes the setting local to the transaction, just like SET LOCAL. That's essential behind a connection pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode: a plain session-level SET would stay on the connection and could be picked up by the next request, from a different tenant. In ORMs like Prisma, Sequelize or TypeORM, open a transaction per request, set the tenant first, then run your queries inside it.

Row-level security turns "every developer must remember the WHERE clause" into "the database won't let anyone forget it". That's the whole point.

What the pool model costs you

  • Noisy neighbours. One heavy tenant can slow everyone down. Mitigate with per-tenant rate limits, read replicas for reports and query timeouts.
  • Per-tenant backup and restore. Restoring one customer's data to yesterday is harder when it's mixed with everyone else's. Plan for logical exports per tenant.
  • Data residency requests. If a customer needs their data in a specific region, they need their own silo, at least for that region.
  • Offboarding. Deleting a tenant means deleting across every table, so keep that logic in one tested place.

The hybrid most mature products end up with

Many SaaS products settle on a tiered model: small and medium customers share a pool, while the largest or most regulated customers get a silo with the same schema. Because the schema is identical, the application code doesn't change; only the connection it uses for that tenant does. Designing for this from the start (a tenants table that records where each tenant lives) costs almost nothing and keeps the door open.

Mistakes we've seen (and made)

  1. Background jobs without tenant context. Queues and scheduled jobs don't come from a web request, so they need to set the tenant explicitly too.
  2. Caches keyed without the tenant. A cache key like "dashboard-stats" will happily serve one company's numbers to another. Include the tenant in every key.
  3. Shared file paths. Uploaded files need tenant-scoped paths and access checks, just like rows.
  4. Analytics with a superuser. Reporting jobs that run as a privileged role skip RLS entirely. Give them their own role and policies.
  5. Unique constraints without tenant_id. They leak information ("this email is taken") and block legitimate data in other tenants.

Which model should you choose?

Your situation Start with
Many small or medium business customers, self-serve sign-up Pool with row-level security
Tens of customers, each with heavy customisation Bridge, or pool with per-tenant configuration
A handful of enterprise or regulated customers Silo
A mix of all of the above Pool by default, silo for the few who need it

Frequently asked questions

Does row-level security slow PostgreSQL down?

The policy adds a condition to each query. With tenant_id indexed (ideally as the first column of your main indexes) the overhead is usually small, but measure it on your own heaviest queries.

Can I move from a pool to a silo later?

Yes, if every tenant-owned row carries tenant_id and your application looks up where each tenant's data lives. Moving a tenant then becomes an export, an import and a routing change.

Is schema-per-tenant a good middle ground?

It works well for tens or a few hundred tenants. Beyond that, running every migration once per schema and the growth of PostgreSQL's catalogs start to hurt.

Do ORMs support row-level security?

They don't need special support. Open a transaction per request, call set_config with the tenant id and local scope, then run your ORM queries inside that transaction.

Should every table have tenant_id?

Every table that holds tenant-owned data, yes, even when you could reach the tenant through a join. It keeps policies simple and indexes effective.

Planning a SaaS product and want a second opinion on its data model? We design and build multi-tenant SaaS platforms. Get in touch and we'll walk through it with you.

title: A React Inbox Adapter for Reliable Email Tests
description:
A React Inbox Adapter for Reliable Email Tests

Email verification tests often become flaky at the boundary between a React screen and a real inbox. The component submits a form, a test starts polling, a message arrives at an unpredictable moment, and suddenly the failure report says only “verification timed out.” That is not much help when the signup flow has five async states.

I have had better results by treating the inbox as an adapter with a small contract. The React component owns user-facing state. A TypeScript service owns polling and message matching. The test owns assertions and cleanup. That separation makes the feature easier to ship and the failure easier to explain.

Why the inbox should be an adapter

An email provider has its own API, timing, retention rules, and odd response shapes. Those details should not leak into a button click handler or a Playwright fixture. The adapter gives the rest of the app a stable vocabulary:

export type VerificationMessage = {
  id: string;
  receivedAt: string;
  verificationUrl: string;
};

export type Inbox = {
  address: string;
  waitForVerification: (options?: { timeoutMs?: number }) => Promise<VerificationMessage>;
  dispose: () => Promise<void>;
};

This interface is intentionally boring. It does not expose provider-specific cursors or ask React to understand whether a 404 means “not arrived yet.” That sounds small, but it remove a surprising amount of branching from the UI and test code.

For a test that needs a temporary email generator, the provider can be swapped behind this interface. The test still receives an address, waits for one matching message, and disposes the inbox when the run finishes.

Define matching and timeout behavior

Polling needs more than a while loop. Define the message boundary before writing the request code:

type PollOptions = {
  after: number;
  timeoutMs: number;
  intervalMs: number;
};

function isVerificationMessage(message: VerificationMessage) {
  return message.verificationUrl.includes("/verify");
}

The after timestamp prevents an old message from satisfying a new signup. A bounded timeout prevents a stuck provider from holding the whole suite forever. In my experience, a retry budget are more useful than an aggressive polling interval: fast requests do not fix an inbox with delayed delivery.

The adapter can return a typed error when the deadline is reached. Include the address, last cursor, elapsed time, and message count in diagnostic data, while keeping tokens and full message bodies out of logs. If the message arrive after the deadline, the report should say that clearly rather than pretending the verification URL was invalid.

Keep polling outside the component

React should receive a promise or a result, not coordinate every timer. A hook can model the user-facing states without knowing how messages are fetched:

type VerificationState =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "waiting"; address: string }
  | { status: "verified"; at: string }
  | { status: "failed"; message: string };

function VerificationStatus({ state }: { state: VerificationState }) {
  if (state.status === "idle") return <p>Ready to verify</p>;
  if (state.status === "waiting") return <p>Check {state.address}</p>;
  if (state.status === "verified") return <p>Verified at {state.at}</p>;
  return <p role="alert">Verification failed: {state.message}</p>;
}

The screen can now handle loading, success, and error states consistently. It also make accessibility work more direct: the waiting message can use a polite live region, while a timeout can use an alert without exposing provider internals.

For recovery flows, I also like to keep the proof path visible in the test result. This pairs well with a failure map for matrix jobs, because each browser or Node.js run can report its own inbox state instead of collapsing everything into one red job.

Make cleanup and evidence first-class

An inbox is test data with a lifetime. Create it with a run ID, record its creation time, and dispose it in a finally block:

const inbox = await createInbox({ runId });

try {
  await completeSignup(inbox.address);
  const message = await inbox.waitForVerification({ timeoutMs: 30_000 });
  await openVerificationUrl(message.verificationUrl);
} finally {
  await inbox.dispose();
}

The cleanup path should run after assertion failures too. If the provider supports a throwaway email generator, use a run-scoped address and keep its retention shorter than the test data retention window. Never put a live verification token in a screenshot, CI annotation, or shared log.

The same idea applies to API design: idempotency for signup APIs helps ensure a retry does not create a second account while the email test is still waiting. The inbox contract and signup contract should agree on a run identifier, so a failure can be followed across both sides.

A practical review checklist

Before merging an email test helper, check:

  • Does each run get a fresh, run-scoped address?
  • Is old mail excluded with a timestamp or cursor?
  • Are timeout and retry behavior explicit?
  • Does the error include useful evidence without secrets?
  • Does cleanup happen in a finally block?
  • Can the React component render the states without provider knowledge?
  • Are test addresses like temp gamil com handled as ordinary fixture data, rather than silently corrected?

If one of these answers is unclear, the test may still pass locally, but it will be harder to trust in CI. A short contract usually fixes that faster than adding another retry.

Final thoughts

Reliable email verification tests are less about polling faster and more about choosing a clean boundary. Keep provider behavior in a TypeScript adapter, keep React focused on visible states, and return evidence that explains the deadline, cursor, and cleanup result. The result is easier to review and easier to maintain when the inbox service changes.

It is a modest bit of architecture, but it lets a team ship signup improvements with less confusion—and fewer mysterious red builds.

title: Your AWS account has more admins than the IAM console shows
description:
Open IAM, filter by the AdministratorAccess policy, and you get a list. Three
users, maybe a role or two. That is the list that gets reviewed in access
reviews, pasted into compliance evidence, and shown to auditors.

It is almost always wrong, and not by a little.

Admin is not a policy you have. It is a state you can reach. Plenty of
principals that are nowhere near that filtered list can reach it in one API
call.

Permissions that grant permissions

Most policy review looks for wide permissions: s3:*, ec2:*, a Resource of
*. Those are worth finding. But there is a second category that gets almost no
attention, and it is the one that matters more: permissions that let you change
permissions.

Here are the ones I keep running into.

iam:CreatePolicyVersion. If you can create a new version of a policy and
set it as the default, you can rewrite any policy you are attached to. Your
tightly scoped policy becomes * on * in a single call. The policy document
that was reviewed last quarter is not the policy document in effect.

iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:AttachRolePolicy, iam:AttachGroupPolicy.
The direct version. If you can attach a policy, you can attach
AdministratorAccess. To yourself.

iam:PutUserPolicy and iam:PutRolePolicy. The same thing with inline
policies, and these are worse because inline policies do not show up where
people look for attached managed policies.

iam:PassRole combined with a compute service. This one is the most common
and the least understood. PassRole on its own does nothing. Combined with
lambda:CreateFunction and lambda:InvokeFunction, or with
ec2:RunInstances, it means you can start something that runs as a role more
privileged than you, and then use it. The permission you needed was not admin.
It was the ability to hand a role to a service.

iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy. You cannot assume that role today. You can
edit its trust policy to say that you can, and then you can.

iam:CreateAccessKey on another user. Mint a key for someone more
privileged and use it. No exploit, no escalation, just an API call that is
working as designed.

iam:CreateLoginProfile and iam:UpdateLoginProfile. Set a console
password on a user who does not have one, or change one that does.

None of these say admin. Every one of them is a path to it.

Why linters miss this

Policy linters are built to answer "is this permission too broad". They flag
wildcards, they flag Resource: *, they score things against least privilege.

iam:CreatePolicyVersion on one specific policy ARN is not broad. It is narrow,
specific, and looks like exactly what a well-scoped policy should look like. It
will pass every check you run and it is a full escalation to whatever that
policy can be rewritten to grant.

The question a linter asks is about the shape of a permission. The question that
matters is about what the permission leads to. Those are different questions and
the second one is a graph problem.

Going and looking

Start by listing what actually exists rather than what you remember granting:

# every inline policy on every role, where the escalation paths usually hide
aws iam list-roles --query 'Roles[].RoleName' --output text \
  | tr '\t' '\n' \
  | while read -r r; do
      aws iam list-role-policies --role-name "$r" \
        --query "PolicyNames[] | [?length(@)>\`0\`]" --output text \
        | grep -q . && echo "$r"
    done

Then search your policy documents for the specific actions above. Not for
wildcards. For iam:PassRole, iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachRolePolicy
and the rest, by name. Anything that holds one of them is effectively an admin
with extra steps, and should be reviewed as an admin.

Two things that make this harder than it sounds. Inline policies are invisible
in most tooling and most dashboards, so they are where this accumulates.
And iam:PassRole is so routine in CI setups that it is usually granted without
anyone asking which roles can be passed, which is the only part that matters.

The number that is actually useful

Stop counting principals with AdministratorAccess. Start counting principals
that can become an administrator, in any number of steps, using only calls they
are already allowed to make.

That number is bigger. On every account I have looked at, it has been bigger.
And unlike the first number, it is the one that describes your actual blast
radius.

If you want to see the trust half of the same picture, who can get into the
account from outside rather than what they can become once in, I maintain a
read-only CLI for it called frontdoor.
It is Apache 2.0, needs no account, and covers AWS, GCP and Azure.

If you review IAM differently, particularly if you have found a clean way to
handle PassRole scoping in CI, I would like to hear it.
