title: Our activation screen asks the local server where the website is, then hardcodes the price anyway
description:
Unactivated, Notifio is one screen: an email field, a token field, a button. It is 130 lines of React in the Electron renderer, and it is the only thing between somebody who has paid and the app they paid for, so it has had more attention per line than anything else in the project.

Two of the decisions in it are good and one of them is a wart I only looked at properly while writing this.

The checks that happen before the network does 

async function handleSubmit(e: FormEvent) {
  e.preventDefault();
  setError("");

  const trimmedEmail = email.trim();
  const trimmedToken = token.trim().toUpperCase();

  if (!trimmedEmail || !trimmedEmail.includes("@")) {
    setError("Enter a valid email address.");
    return;
  }
  if (!trimmedToken || trimmedToken.length < 10) {
    setError("Enter your activation token.");
    return;
  }

  setLoading(true);
  const { ok, data } = await activateLicense(trimmedEmail, trimmedToken);
  setLoading(false);

  if (!ok) {
    setError(data.error || "Activation failed. Please try again.");
    return;
  }

  onActivated();
}

Three guards, and none of them is the real validation. activateLicense posts to a local HTTP endpoint in the Electron main process, that endpoint repeats the same two checks, and only then does it ask our server whether the pair exists:

app.post('/api/license/activate', async (req, res) => {
  const { email, token } = req.body;

  if (!email || !email.includes('@')) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Valid email is required.' });
  }
  if (!token || token.length < 10) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Valid token is required.' });
  }

  const normalEmail = email.trim().toLowerCase();
  const normalToken = token.trim().toUpperCase();

  // Validate against server. A licence is only wrong if the server says so:
  // telling someone to check their activation email because their wifi was
  // down sends them looking for a problem that is not there.
  const check = await monitor.checkLicense(normalEmail, normalToken);
  if (!check.ok && check.reason === 'unreachable') {
    return res.status(503).json({ error: 'Could not reach notifio.app to check that licence. ...' });
  }
  if (!check.ok) {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Invalid email or token. Please check your activation email.' });
  }
  // ...
});

Three layers, two of which run on the user's own machine. That looks like one copy too many until you notice that the renderer is not the only thing that can reach a local server listening on 127.0.0.1, so the main process cannot treat its own UI as trusted input. And the remote answer is the only one that decides anything: note the 503 for unreachable, kept distinct from the 403 for wrong, because a failure to ask is not a no.

So why does the renderer check at all?

An activation screen is the one place in the app where the user is most likely to be in a bad mood already. They have paid, they have switched windows to find the email, they have copied something out of it. A round trip that comes back to say the field is empty is the worst available answer, because it is slow, it is network-dependent, and the user already knows.

The length check is the one that earns its keep. Tokens look like NTFIO-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX, which is eighteen characters, so anything under ten is not a token that was ever issued: it is half a paste, or a confirmation number, or the word "token". Rejecting it locally turns a round trip into an instant answer. Note that the floor is ten and not eighteen, and it does not check the alphabet either, deliberately: a client that knows the exact token format has to be updated when the format changes, and the server would still be the one to say no. A loose floor catches the mistakes people actually make without encoding anything.

The email check is one character. includes("@") catches the genuinely empty and the obviously-not-an-address, and leaves everything else to the layers behind it, in the same spirit as the deliberately loose regex on our contact form. The failure mode worth avoiding is not "a malformed address reached the server". It is a paying customer with a perfectly valid address that our regex dislikes.

Uppercasing at submit, not while typing 

const trimmedToken = token.trim().toUpperCase();

The token alphabet has no O, no 0, no I and no 1, which I wrote about in the post on why 32 characters makes the maths safe. It is also uppercase, and the server uppercases what it receives before looking it up.

Notice where the client transform is: in the submit handler, not in onChange. Uppercasing on every keystroke means writing back into controlled state mid-edit, which is how you get a cursor that jumps to the end when someone fixes a character in the middle. Doing it in text-transform: uppercase has the opposite failure: the field looks uppercase and submits whatever was typed, so the only consistent thing about it is that it is lying to you.

Transforming at the boundary leaves the input alone while it is being edited and normalises once, at the moment the value stops being a half-typed string and becomes a request.

<input
  id="token"
  placeholder="NTFIO-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX"
  value={token}
  onChange={(e) => setToken(e.target.value)}
  autoComplete="off"
  spellCheck={false}
  style={{ fontFamily: "monospace" }}
/>

spellCheck={false} and autoComplete="off" are both there for the same reason: a password manager or a spell checker offering suggestions over a field full of random characters is noise at the worst moment. Monospace is so that a user comparing the field against their email can do it character by character without counting.

The email field above it does the opposite, autoComplete="email", because that one is a real email address and the browser knows it better than the user remembers it.

The link that asks where it should point 

const [pricingLink, setPricingLink] = useState("https://notifio.app/pricing");

useEffect(() => {
  getServerUrl().then(({ data }) => {
    setPricingLink(`${data.url}/pricing`);
  });
}, []);

The renderer has no preload script and no build-time environment variables. It talks to a local HTTP server in the main process, which is a design I have written about in our Electron renderer has no preload script, and one of those endpoints exists purely to answer this question:

app.get('/api/server-url', (req, res) => {
  const url = (process.env.NOTIFIO_SERVER_URL || 'https://notifio.app').replace(/\/$/, '');
  res.json({ url });
});

So a development build points the "get a licence" link at a local Next.js instance, and a packaged build points it at production, with no conditional in the component and no isDev reaching the renderer. The trailing slash strip is there because the caller builds the URL with template interpolation, and https://notifio.app//pricing is the kind of link that works everywhere except in a screenshot.

The useState default is the interesting bit. It is the production URL, hardcoded, so the link is already correct before the request resolves. That means the component renders a usable link on frame one, and the fetch only ever corrects it for the developer. The same string is therefore written down twice, once here and once as the server's fallback, and the one on the server is the one that matters.

I think that duplication is worth it for the first render, but it is duplication, and I would not defend a third copy.

The wart 

<p className="mt-5 text-center text-[13px] text-[#525252]">
  Don't have a license?{" "}
  <a href={pricingLink} className="text-[#a3a3a3] underline">
    Get one for £20
  </a>
</p>

That price is a string literal in a desktop app.

On the website, the same number comes out of one constant:

export const PRICE_CURRENCY = "gbp";
export const LICENSE_PRICE_PENCE = 2000;

which is the amount Stripe charges, the figure in the page's structured data, and the input to the currency localisation that shows a visitor in Berlin an approximate euro price on notifio.app/pricing. One number, one source, several renderings.

The app does not participate in any of that, and the consequences split cleanly into one that does not matter and one that does.

The one that does not matter: the app says pounds to everybody, including people who will see euros on the website. That is defensible, because pounds is what the card is actually charged, so the app is quoting the real figure and the website is quoting a converted approximation of it.

The one that does: a price change means shipping a new build of a desktop app with no auto-update. The website would update in a deploy and the app would keep saying £20 until every user re-downloaded it. That is not a theoretical risk, it is the reason the website derives it from a constant in the first place, and the app is the only surface that opted out.

The fix is small and obvious, which is why it is embarrassing rather than interesting: the component already makes an HTTP call to ask where the website is. It could ask what the licence costs in the same breath, and the endpoint it is already calling is in the same file as the one that would answer. I am writing it down here partly so I actually do it.

Try the screen

The installers are at notifio.app/download, the price this post is about is on notifio.app/pricing, and the activation steps, including what to do when the email with the token has gone missing, are at notifio.app/help.

If you open the app without a licence, the screen in this post is the first thing you get. The field with the monospace font is the one that has had the arguments.

title: Launching a Tiny Free Tool: Lessons from Building Instagram Grid Maker
description:
I recently built a tiny free tool called Instagram Grid Maker.

The idea is simple: upload one image, choose a grid layout like 3x1, 3x2, or 3x3, preview the crop, then download numbered PNG tiles for posting to Instagram.

It is not a huge SaaS product. There is no login, no dashboard, no team workspace, no complex onboarding flow.

And that was exactly the point.

Here are a few lessons I learned while building it.

1. Small tools still need real product thinking

At first, I thought the main feature was “split an image into tiles.”

But once I started using the tool myself, I realized the actual user problem was more specific:

“I want to post this image as an Instagram grid, and I don’t want to mess up the order.”

That changed the product decisions.

The preview needed to show the final grid clearly. The downloaded files needed numbered names. The UI needed to explain which tile should be uploaded first. A simple image splitter became a workflow tool.

The lesson: even tiny tools need to understand the user’s real anxiety.

2. Browser-based processing is a feature, not just an implementation detail

For this kind of tool, users may upload personal photos, product images, brand assets, or campaign visuals.

So I wanted the core workflow to happen in the browser instead of requiring an account or server upload.

That decision shaped the whole product:

  • faster first use
  • no sign-up wall
  • less privacy concern
  • lower infrastructure complexity
  • easier positioning as a free utility

Sometimes the technical constraint becomes part of the value proposition.

3. Free tools need fewer distractions

When people search for a tool like this, they usually want to finish a job quickly.

They do not want to read a long homepage, compare pricing tiers, or create an account before seeing whether the tool works.

So I tried to make the first screen do the job immediately: upload, choose layout, preview, export.

A tiny tool should respect the user’s momentum.

4. UX details matter more than feature count

The most useful details were not the biggest features.

They were things like:

  • layout presets for common grid sizes
  • custom rows and columns
  • crop preview before export
  • numbered output files
  • ZIP download
  • a safe export option for taller Instagram posts

None of these sound impressive by themselves. But together, they make the tool feel calmer and harder to misuse.

That is often the difference between a “script with a UI” and a product.

5. SEO pages should help users decide

For small free tools, SEO matters. But I don’t think SEO pages should only be keyword containers.

A good page should answer the questions users already have:

  • What size should my image be?
  • Should I use a 3x1, 3x2, or 3x3 grid?
  • What happens after I download the tiles?
  • Which order should I upload them in?
  • Is this better as a grid or carousel?

When the content genuinely helps the user complete the task, SEO and product education start working together.

6. Launching small is underrated

It is tempting to keep adding features before launch.

But small tools benefit from being shipped early because real usage reveals what matters.

Before launch, I could guess what users needed. After launch, I could see which pages they found, which layouts mattered, and which explanations reduced confusion.

The product became clearer by being public.

Final thought

Building a tiny free tool reminded me that useful software does not always need to be big.

Sometimes a good product is just:

  • one clear job
  • a fast workflow
  • no unnecessary friction
  • enough polish that users trust it

That was the goal with Instagram Grid Maker, and it is a pattern I want to reuse for future small tools.

title: A Reviewable Voice-Selection Contract for TTS Interfaces
description:
A Reviewable Voice-Selection Contract for TTS Interfaces

Voice is often added after the edit, but it changes what a listener understands before the visuals have finished. A useful brief starts with the scene: who speaks, what must be clear, and what emotion belongs in the line.

Begin with a small audition

Write one statement, one question, one proper noun, and one sentence with a pause. Use the same script for every candidate. Siri AI Voice can be evaluated for an assistant-like direction, Sonic.EXE AI Voice for a clearly fictional character context, and Soundwave AI Voice for a technical or mechanical atmosphere. These are candidate roles, not proof of quality, affiliation, or permission.

Review the mix, not only the sample

Listen once with music and effects, then again with the voice alone. A dramatic voice can bury an important noun; a plain voice can become the better choice when the picture and pacing arrive. Save the script version, pronunciation notes, selected candidate, and the reason it was accepted.

Keep the boundary visible

A label resembling a known assistant or character does not establish an official relationship. Scripts, music, footage, and voice use can each have separate rights. A preview is an audition, not legal clearance.

A reusable workflow

  1. Define the listener and the scene job.
  2. Generate identical test lines.
  3. Check names, numbers, pauses, and intelligibility.
  4. Compare in the final mix.
  5. Store the decision with the audio file.

VideoAI can organize these experiments, but the creative decision remains human. Choose the voice that helps the scene do its work; let style support the story rather than replace it.

title: Before an AI agent acts, show me what it can change
description:
“Allow this action” is a difficult question to answer when I can’t see what the action actually does.

Which file will change? Who will receive the message? Is the agent preparing a draft, or sending it?

Before I approve an action, I want those details in front of me.

I’m KAT, co-founder of 123sudo. I work on product experience, creative direction, and growth. A recent conversation here on DEV got me thinking about what an understandable approval screen should show.

This is a product-design perspective, not a security specification or an announcement of existing features in our AI workspace, 9xchat.

Connected doesn’t mean approved

Connecting a tool makes certain actions available. It shouldn’t make the user guess which of those actions an agent is about to take.

An email tool might let an agent:

  • Read a message.
  • Prepare a reply.
  • Save a draft.
  • Send the reply.

Those are different outcomes.

The same goes for files. Reading a document is different from overwriting it.

I’d want the interface to distinguish between:

This tool is connected.

And:

This action is permitted for the current task.

That distinction matters more to me than a long list of integration names.

Show the outcome, not just the tool

A technical tool name may help a developer understand what’s happening. It may tell another user very little.

Compare these two approval requests:

Allow send_message?

And:

Send this email to Alex at an external address, with the attached project brief?

The second gives me something I can check.

For an email, I’d want to see:

  • The sender account.
  • The recipient, including CC and BCC.
  • The subject and message.
  • Any attachments.
  • Whether the action sends immediately or saves a draft.

For a file edit, I’d want:

  • The target file and its location.
  • The proposed changes.
  • Whether it creates, edits, or overwrites something.
  • Any relevant limits on undoing the action.

The preview should answer a simple question:

What will be different after I click approve?

Build the preview from the pending action

Someone in the DEV discussion made a useful distinction: the preview should come from the tool call itself, not just the agent’s summary.

That changed how I thought about the interface.

An agent might say:

I’ll send the brief to Alex.

But the pending action contains the details that matter: the actual address, message, and attachments.

A reassuring explanation isn’t enough if it doesn’t match those details.

My design preference would be to show a readable explanation alongside the relevant fields from the pending action.

The explanation helps me understand. The fields help me verify.

And that preview alone isn’t a guarantee. The system still needs to enforce that the approved action is the one executed.

Approval should belong to a specific action

Imagine I approve a message.

Then the agent changes the recipient, adds an attachment, or rewrites the body.

Does my earlier approval still apply?

For changes like those, I’d expect a fresh approval.

Otherwise, I’m approving one thing and potentially getting another.

This is a principle I’d want the system to enforce, not just a promise written on the button:

Approve this action, with these details.

Warnings need words, not just colours

A coloured border might draw attention to an external recipient or a file outside the task folder.

But colour alone shouldn’t carry the meaning.

I’d pair it with a clear label:

  • External recipient
  • Outside the selected task folder
  • Overwrites an existing file

Then explain why it matters.

For example:

This attachment will be sent to an address outside your organisation.

That tells me what I’m deciding. A red icon by itself doesn’t.

More prompts don’t automatically mean more control

I don’t want an approval dialog for every tiny step.

If every action gets the same warning, the interface risks teaching people to click through without reading.

I’d rather see understandable boundaries at the start of a task, followed by specific approval requests when the agent reaches an action outside those boundaries.

For example:

You can read the selected files and prepare a draft. Ask before editing files or sending messages.

That’s easier to reason about than an unexplained “full access” setting.

The right boundary will depend on the task, the sensitivity of the information, and the tool. Reading can matter too, especially when private information is involved.

What I’d want to see before execution

My starting checklist would be:

  1. Access: What information can the agent read?
  2. Actions: What can it create, change, send, or delete?
  3. Targets: Which accounts, recipients, files, or folders are involved?
  4. Approval: Which actions require me to review the exact details?
  5. Changes: What happens if the action changes after I approve it?

This isn’t a complete security model. It’s a way to make the user’s decision less vague.

Clear previews still need reliable permission checks and execution controls behind them.

Trust needs something concrete to check

As a co-founder helping shape an AI workspace, I’m interested in interfaces that make an agent’s actions understandable.

Not because the agent should explain every internal step.

Because when it changes something on my behalf, I should understand the change.

“Trust me” isn’t a useful approval screen.

Show me the action. Show me the target. Let me check what matters.

Disclosure: I’m a co-founder of 123sudo, the team behind 9xchat. These are design principles I’m exploring, not claims about features currently available in the product.

AI helped structure and draft this article.

What would you need to see before approving an AI agent’s action?

title: How to QA a translation in a language you can't read
description:
I ship in ten languages. I speak two of them.

For a long time my quality process was "the translator seemed competent," which is not a process, it is a hope. Here is the system I use now. None of it requires me to read the target language.

Separate the translator from the reviewer

This is the single highest-value change, and it is organisational rather than technical.

Nobody is a reliable reviewer of their own work, and that is doubly true in translation, where the translator has already made a hundred interpretive decisions they have stopped being able to see. One person translates. A different native speaker reviews. They should not be the same person and ideally should not be in the same room.

If budget only allows one native speaker per language, spend them on review and use a lower-cost first pass for the draft. Reviewing a flawed translation is faster than producing a good one, and the output is better than one unreviewed expert pass.

Automate everything that doesn't need a human

A surprising share of translation defects are mechanical, and mechanical defects can be caught by a script that does not speak the language either. I run all of these in CI against the translated resource files:

  • Placeholder integrity. Every placeholder in the source exists in the target, with the same name, and no extras. This is the single most common serious bug, and it crashes at runtime rather than reading oddly.
  • ICU syntax validity. Plural and select blocks parse, and the categories present are the ones that locale actually requires. A translation missing a required plural category will fall back silently and look fine until the number is right.
  • Untranslated strings. Target identical to source, across a whole file, usually means a pipeline failure rather than a word that happens to be the same.
  • Length budget. Flag anything substantially longer than source. It will not throw, it will just overflow a button somewhere you aren't looking.
  • Terminology adherence. If you have a glossary — and you should — check that the agreed term was actually used. This one catches real meaning drift, not just mechanics.
  • Punctuation and spacing conventions. Some locales take a space before a colon, some use different quotation marks, some use a different decimal separator. These are rule-checkable.

None of this tells you whether the translation is good. All of it tells you whether it is broken, and it removes the broken ones from the human reviewer's plate so their attention goes where it is actually needed.

Review in context, never in a spreadsheet

Translators are usually handed a column of strings with no indication of where any of them appear. Then we are surprised when a word that means "free of charge" shows up where we meant "unoccupied."

Give the reviewer the actual screens. A build, a staging link, or at minimum a screenshot attached to each string. The defects that only show up in context — wrong register, wrong sense of an ambiguous word, a button label that is grammatically fine and situationally absurd — are exactly the ones that automation cannot catch and that users notice first.

If you do nothing else from this post, do this one. It is the highest ratio of quality gained to effort spent of anything I have tried.

Give the review a rubric

"Does this look right?" produces a thumbs up. Ask four separate questions and you get usable answers:

  1. Accuracy. Does it say what the source says?
  2. Terminology. Does it use the agreed terms from the glossary?
  3. Register. Is the formality level right and consistent? Does it address the reader the way we intend to?
  4. Fluency. Would a native speaker write it this way, or does it read as translated?

Scoring those separately matters because they have different fixes and different severities. A fluency complaint is a polish item. An accuracy or terminology failure is a bug.

Sample, don't boil the ocean

Full review of every string on every release does not survive contact with a shipping schedule.

I review everything once at launch for a locale, then sample afterwards — weighted toward strings that are new, strings that changed, and strings on screens that matter most. If a sample comes back with defects above your tolerance, widen it for that locale. If it comes back clean repeatedly, narrow it.

The point is that you are measuring translation quality as an ongoing property, not certifying it once and assuming it holds.

Back-translation is weaker than it looks

A common suggestion is to have the target translated back into English and compare. I use it rarely and trust it less than I used to.

It catches gross errors — a flipped negation, a dropped clause. It is poor at everything subtler, because a fluent back-translator will unconsciously repair an awkward target, and an awkward back-translator will make a perfectly good target look wrong. You end up investigating noise.

Use it as a spot check on your highest-stakes strings. Do not build a quality process on it.

The thing I wish someone had told me earlier: you cannot eyeball your way out of not speaking the language, and you do not have to. Almost everything above is either a script or an organisational decision. The part that genuinely requires a native speaker is smaller than it first appears — but it is not zero, and the mistake is pretending it is.

title: How to Improve SaaS Onboarding Video Experience for Better Retention?
description:
The first five minutes of a user’s interaction with your SaaS product are more important than the last five months of your marketing campaign.
You’ve spent thousands of dollars on SaaS lead generation and SEO to get them to sign up. They are finally in. But then, silence. They click around, get confused, and close the tab, never to return.

This is the "Silent Killer" of software growth. In 2026, the average SaaS product loses 40% to 60% of users immediately after a single session. Why? Because the onboarding experience felt like reading a 500-page manual instead of a guided tour.

If you want to stop the "leaky bucket" and boost your Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), you need to master the art of the first impression. Here is your expert blueprint to transforming SaaS onboarding from a hurdle into a growth engine.

  1. The Psychology of Onboarding: Why First Impressions Are Sticky Onboarding isn't just a product walkthrough; it’s a psychological transition. Your user is moving from "Problem Aware" to "Solution Relieved."

The Concept of Time to Value (TTV)
The most critical metric in 2026 is Time to Value (TTV). This is the duration it takes for a new user to realize the "Aha! Moment"—that specific second where they understand exactly how your tool solves their
problem.

Short TTV: High retention, high dopamine, high brand loyalty.
Long TTV: High churn, frustration, and a wasted acquisition cost.

Cognitive Load vs. Guidance
Humans have a finite amount of mental energy. If your dashboard throws 20 pop-ups at a user the moment they log in, you’ve increased their cognitive load to the breaking point. Effective onboarding uses Progressive
Disclosure, showing only what is necessary at that specific moment.

  1. Mapping the "Aha! Moment" for Different User Personas Not every user signs up for the same reason. A manager might want high-level reports, while an executive assistant wants automated scheduling.

Segmented Onboarding Paths
In 2026, "one size fits all" is dead. You should implement a Choose Your Own Adventure style of onboarding:

The Quick Setup: For users who want the bare minimum to get started.

The Power User: For those who want to integrate every API and customize
every setting.

The Team Lead: For those focused on inviting members and setting permissions.

By asking 2–3 simple questions during the signup flow, you can tailor the entire dashboard experience to the user’s specific goals, drastically reducing early-stage friction.

  1. The 5 Pillars of a World-Class Onboarding Flow To build an experience that keeps users coming back, you must integrate these five elements:

A. The "Empty State" Optimization
Nothing is more intimidating than a blank dashboard with 0% data. Instead of showing "No Data Found," use Sample Data or Placeholders. Show the user what success looks like.

Give them a "dummy" project to play with so they can learn the features without the fear of breaking their own real-world data.

B. Interactive Walkthroughs (Not Static Tours)
Static "Next-Next-Finish" tours are often ignored. Instead, use Event-Triggered Tooltips.

Bad: A tour that highlights the "Upload" button even if the user isn't ready.

Good: A tooltip that appears only when the user hovers over the project area, saying, "Click here to upload your first file and see the magic happen!"

C. Gamified Checklists
Human brains love crossing things off a list. A progress bar that starts at 20% (because they already completed the "Sign Up" and "Email Verification" steps) creates a "Zeigarnik Effect"—a psychological phenomenon where people remember uncompleted tasks better than completed ones, pushing them to reach 100%.

D. High-Quality Explainer Videos
As we’ve seen in our recent guide on How to Reduce SaaS Churn Rate Fast, video content is king for activation.

A 60-second video embedded in the onboarding flow can explain a complex feature better than ten paragraphs of text.

E. In-App Messaging & Human Touchpoints
For B2B SaaS, a "Welcome" message from a real person (or a very well-calibrated AI bot) can bridge the gap.

If a user gets stuck on a specific step for more than 2 minutes, trigger a live chat prompt: "Hey! I noticed you're setting up the CRM sync. Need a hand?"

  1. Reducing Friction: The "Less is More" Philosophy Every form field you add to your signup process reduces your conversion rate by roughly 10%.

Frictionless Signup
Social Sign-On (SSO): Google, Slack, and LinkedIn logins are no longer optional—they are expected.

Deferred Verification: Let users enter the product before they have to verify their email. Let them feel the value first; they’ll be much more likely to verify their account once they’ve seen what’s inside.

The "Frictionless" Paradox
Sometimes, good friction is necessary. If your product requires a complex setup (like installing a tracking code), adding a "Technical Setup Wizard" that guides them through it step-by-step is better than letting them figure it out alone.

  1. Post-Onboarding: The Retention Phase Onboarding doesn't end after the first login. It continues until the user becomes a "Habitual User."

Lifecycle Email Sequences
Don't just send "We miss you" emails. Send Value-Based Emails:

Day 1: Welcome + First Step.

Day 3: "Did you know?" (Feature highlight).

Day 7: Case study of a user similar to them.

Day 10: Personalized "Pro-Tip" based on their actual usage data.

Feedback Loops
If a user completes the onboarding, ask them: "On a scale of 1-10, how easy was it to get started?" If they drop out, use an automated "Exit Intent" survey. This data is the most valuable SEO and Product asset you own.

  1. Measuring Success: Metrics That Matter in 2026 You can't improve what you don't measure. Focus on these User Engagement Metrics:

Activation Rate: The % of users who reach the "Aha! Moment."
Completion Rate: The % of users who finish the onboarding checklist.

D1, D7, and D30 Retention: How many users come back after 1 day, 7 days, and a month?

Feature Adoption Rate: Are they using the core features, or just scratching the surface?

Conclusion: Onboarding is Your Best Growth Strategy
In the competitive world of 2026, your software’s features are easily replicable, but your User Experience (UX) is not.

A seamless, personalized, and fast-paced onboarding flow transforms curious signups into paying advocates.

Stop looking at onboarding as a technical necessity and start viewing it as the ultimate marketing funnel. When you reduce the friction between "Hello" and "Value," growth becomes inevitable.

title: Designing honest loading and empty states for a rank-checking interface
description:
This article was prepared with AI assistance. It proposes a design checklist for a hypothetical rank-checking interface; it does not describe a deployed product, a user study, or measured performance results.

A search measurement interface often looks simple in its successful state: a query, a result, and perhaps a page address. The harder design work starts when the interface has no result to show. A request may still be running, the current filters may hide available records, or a check may finish without finding the expected page within its scope. Treating those situations as one blank panel makes the interface difficult to understand. This article proposes a small state vocabulary that a product team can review before building the screen.

Begin with what the application actually knows

Write a sentence for each state before choosing an icon or illustration. An idle screen can say that no check has been requested. A loading screen can say that a request is in progress. A completed check can display its result alongside the conditions used. A failed request can say that the application could not complete the check. These sentences express different facts. The implementation should preserve those differences rather than deriving all display copy from whether a result array currently contains items.

For a hypothetical tool, define idle, validating, loading, completed, failed, and cancelled as separate review cases. Your real application may need different cases, but every additional state should answer a concrete user question. Avoid adding categories merely because a state diagram can accommodate them. Ask what the user can do next, what information remains trustworthy, and what the application cannot yet conclude. This exercise turns an empty screen into an explicit product decision that designers, developers, and reviewers can discuss together.

Keep a previous result attached to its original request

Consider a user who checks one query and then starts a second check. If the first result remains on screen, label it as the previous result while the new request runs. Otherwise, the user may read an old page address under a newly edited query. One practical layout is to show the submitted query and its conditions inside the result card, while keeping the editable form above it. The card then describes the observation that produced it rather than whatever text currently occupies the form.

Choose a clear rule for replacing that card. You might retain it until a new request succeeds, or replace it immediately with a loading panel. Either choice needs deliberate copy and a review case. If you retain it after a failure, explain that the attempted check failed and the displayed card belongs to an earlier successful request. Do not silently present the earlier card as a fallback result for the failed request. Preserving useful information is helpful only when its origin remains visible.

Separate missing results from request failures

A request failure describes the application's attempt to obtain information. A completed check without the expected page describes an observation made under the check's conditions. The interface should not use the same headline for both. For example, a failure message could explain that the check could not finish and offer a retry. A completed observation could identify the query and scope, then state that the expected page was not found within that scope. The wording should match what the actual method supports.

Avoid turning limited observations into claims about the whole search ecosystem. A hypothetical interface should not infer that a page has disappeared everywhere merely because one check does not return it. Place relevant limits near the result instead of hiding them in a distant help page. If your method checks a bounded set of results, describe that boundary honestly. If a condition is unknown, display it as unknown. The product specification should identify which statement is supported by the available data before anyone writes reassuring or alarming copy.

Give loading messages an end condition

A spinner alone tells the user very little about the task. Pair the loading state with a plain description of the submitted action and make clear whether the user can edit the form, start another request, or cancel. These are product choices rather than universal rules. For a simple interface, preventing a duplicate submission while the same request is active can make the workflow easier to reason about. If parallel requests are supported, provide a way to tell their results apart.

Review what happens when a request takes longer than expected. Do not display a percentage unless the application actually measures progress in a way that supports it. A message such as waiting for the check to finish can be more honest than a fabricated progress bar. Decide how the request reaches a failure or timeout state, and what the user sees at that transition. If cancellation is available, distinguish cancelling the interface workflow from any server operation whose cancellation cannot be guaranteed by the client.

Treat status announcements as part of the interface

Dynamic text should be reviewed with assistive technology as well as visually. MDN describes the ARIA status role as an advisory live region with implicit polite announcement behavior. It also advises against moving focus to that region simply because its content updates. See the MDN status role reference for the underlying behavior. A team's implementation should still be checked in the browsers and assistive technology combinations relevant to its audience.

A practical review case is to submit a check using the keyboard and listen to the resulting announcement. Can the user tell that a check has started and later finished without losing their place? Does the application repeat the entire result table when only a short status message is necessary? Keep the announcement concise and let users explore detailed results in the ordinary page structure. The goal of this review is a coherent interaction, not the presence of a particular attribute in an inspection tool.

Make recovery specific to the problem

A retry button is useful only when retrying has a plausible purpose. If the query is missing, the message should identify the missing input and help the user return to it. If the request failed after valid input, preserve that input so the user does not have to reconstruct it. If active filters produce an empty view of stored records, explain that the filter selection is responsible and offer a clear route to adjusting it. These cases should have different recovery actions.

Avoid generic instructions that send every problem to a support channel. A short message can state what happened, which information remains available, and what the user can try. Do not promise that retrying will succeed. For a persistent failure, you can provide a reference identifier if the application supports one, while keeping technical diagnostics out of ordinary copy. Review whether a proposed recovery action causes duplicate requests or accidentally discards the previous observation. Recovery should be tested as a workflow rather than reviewed only as a button label.

Review transitions, then record decisions

Create a compact review matrix covering an initial visit, a valid submission, invalid input, a slow request, a failed request, an empty filtered view, and a second submission after a successful result. For each case, record the visible statement, available action, preserved information, and focus behavior. Use invented example queries and explicitly label them as fixtures. This makes the review repeatable without exposing customer data or suggesting that the fixture represents actual search behavior.

Finish by recording the decisions that could otherwise remain implicit: whether previous results stay visible, whether cancellation is supported, which conditions appear on a result card, and which empty states have their own messages. Assign an owner to unresolved questions. A clear interface state is a small contract between the application and its user. It says what the application knows at that moment and offers an appropriate next step. That contract is worth designing before polishing the successful result screen.

Project context

We share these interface notes from the SEOLOK account. The SEOLOK rank-checking project provides the context for this proposed checklist; this article does not claim that the described states have been tested in the deployed product.

title: AI can design an app now. Are designers redundant?
description:
AI can now draft a screen, write the button labels, and turn a sketch into a clickable prototype in minutes. So here is the question every designer has quietly asked at 2 a.m.: are designers now redundant?

To answer it honestly, we have to separate two things people often mix up: producing design artefacts and doing design.

  • AI automates the output of design—screens, copy, prototypes—not the decisions behind it.
  • When producing a draft becomes cheap, the bottleneck moves to judgement, context, and validation.
  • Tasks inside the designer’s job will disappear. The job itself will move up a level.
  • The designers at real risk are the ones whose work stops at the artefact.

AI can make the options quickly. Design is deciding which one is right for the people who will use it.

What design actually is

From the outside, design looks like making screens. In practice, a screen is the last and smallest part of the work. A typical app feature passes through five layers:

  1. Problem: Who is the user, what are they trying to do, and what gets in their way?
  2. Priority: Of everything we could build, what matters first, and what do we leave out?
  3. Flow: In what order do things happen, and what happens when something goes wrong?
  4. Interface: Layout, components, hierarchy, copy, and visual style.
  5. Validation: Does it work for real people, in real conditions? What do we change?

Each layer depends on the one before it. A beautiful interface built on the wrong problem is still a failure—just a better-looking one.

What AI is actually good at

Map today’s AI tools onto those layers and a clear pattern appears:

Where AI is strong What it helps with
Interface Drafting layouts, generating variations, writing microcopy, applying a design system, and building quick prototypes.
Problem and validation Summarising reviews and interviews, grouping feedback, and spotting patterns across lots of text.
Priority and flow Still weak at choosing trade-offs, deciding what to cut, and knowing which edge case will hurt users.

AI is strongest at the layer that is easiest to see and weakest at the layers that decide whether a product succeeds. That is why it can look like it replaces designers, while in practice it replaces only part of what they do.

Four reasons designers aren’t redundant

1. Cheap drafts make choosing more important

When one screen took a day, a team might compare two options. When AI produces twenty in a minute, someone has to decide which one is right—and why.

Abundance does not remove the need for judgement; it multiplies it. The scarce skill is no longer making options. It is choosing well between them.

2. AI doesn’t know your user’s context

A model learns from patterns across millions of apps. It has never stood in a supermarket aisle holding a basket in one hand and a phone in the other, which is exactly the situation our Ingredient Scanner has to be designed for.

Context like that changes where buttons go, how big text is, and what appears first. It comes from observing users, not from training data.

A real use case has constraints that a generic prompt cannot see: one hand is busy, the aisle is distracting, and the answer needs to be immediate.

3. AI drifts toward the average

Generative models produce the most likely answer. In design, the most likely answer is the most common one. That is useful for standard patterns such as login screens or settings, but it is the opposite of what makes a product memorable.

Differentiation is a deliberate choice to not do the average thing, and someone has to make it.

4. Someone has to own the result

If a flow confuses older users, if a screen fails accessibility, or if a dark pattern slips into checkout, the question is not “which tool generated this?” but “who approved it?”

Responsibility for the user’s experience cannot be delegated to a model. It needs a person who notices, cares, and can explain the decision.

AI is great at making options. Design is the job of choosing.

Good review connects interface choices to evidence: what users said, what they can access, and what the product needs to achieve.

The strongest counter-argument

To be fair, the case for “designers are redundant” is not silly. It goes like this: most apps do not need original design. They need a decent, standard interface, fast. AI already does that well enough.

This is partly true. For internal tools, simple prototypes, or early MVPs, a developer with a good design system and an AI tool can ship something perfectly usable without a dedicated designer. Some design work—resizing assets, making variants, or writing first-draft copy—will shrink for real.

But that argument proves something narrower than it claims. It shows that certain design tasks are being automated, not that the design role is. As soon as a product competes on experience, serves a specific audience, or carries real risk, the upper layers—problem, priority, flow, and validation—come back. Those are human work.

What actually changes for designers

What becomes more valuable:

  • User research and observing real behaviour
  • Framing problems and setting constraints
  • Building and maintaining a strong design system that AI can follow
  • Critiquing and editing, not just creating
  • Accessibility, ethics, and edge cases

What becomes less valuable:

  • Producing screens from a clear spec
  • Making many variants by hand
  • Pixel-perfect mockups that are never tested
  • Design work that stops at the hand-off

How we work with AI at Nexa Tech

Our rule is simple: AI speeds up the parts we can easily check, and people own the parts that need judgement.

  • Research: AI groups app-store reviews and feedback into themes; a designer reads the raw quotes before drawing conclusions.
  • Exploration: AI generates many layout options; the team picks a direction based on the user’s context, not what looks best in isolation.
  • Production: AI drafts screens from our components and tokens; a designer fixes hierarchy, spacing, and states.
  • Validation: Real users test the prototype. AI can predict behaviour, but only people can show it.

Start with your design system. AI follows whatever rules you give it. A clear, documented design system turns its output from “generic app” into “close to ours,” and makes every review faster.

So, is the designer redundant?

No. But the designer who only pushes pixels might be.

AI has made the visible part of design cheap. That forces the invisible part—understanding people and choosing what to build for them—into the spotlight. Designers who move up to that level will not be replaced by AI. They will be the ones deciding how to use it.

Full Story: https://www.nexateam.dev/blog/ai-in-app-design

title: From zero to NanoClaw (Changelog Interviews #686)
description:
Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private.

They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.

title: Amazon Connect Customer now provides automated checks to improve performance evaluation forms
description:
Amazon Connect Customer now suggests changes to performance evaluation forms that improve the accuracy of evaluations automatically filled by AI. While setting up an evaluation form, managers can run an automated check that compares the form against best practices with a single click. Managers then receive a list of evaluation questions that are missing context for AI to score reliably, along with suggestions to make them more specific. For example, the check might flag "Did the agent provide a sales disclosure?" and prompt the manager to define exactly what the agent must disclose before a sale. This helps managers automatically score human and AI agents fairly and accurately, while spending less time refining their evaluation forms.

This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more, please visit our documentation and our webpage. For information about Amazon Connect Customer pricing, please visit our pricing page.

title: Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
description:
Amazon S3 Vectors metadata pre-filtering is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions. Pre-filtering evaluates metadata filters before running similarity search, returning up to 5x more of the matching vectors when your filter is selective. S3 Vectors also adds a prefix match operator ($startsWith) for filtering on values like paths and URLs. Together, these improvements give your retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agentic, and semantic-search applications more complete results when you filter, so your applications return more relevant answers.

S3 Vectors provides native support to store and query vectors in Amazon S3, delivering purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage and query at billion-vector scale. With this launch, indexes in new vector buckets in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions use metadata pre-filtering by default, with no change to how you write vectors with PutVectors or run filtered queries with QueryVectors. To use pre-filtering on an existing index, update it in place with the UpdateIndexMode API. You can also compare pre-filtering against your current filtering on the same index, using a per-query parameter on QueryVectors, before you update.

Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. We are in the process of deploying this change and plan to complete the deployment in the coming days. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation and the AWS News blog.

title: AWS Lambda supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event sources
description:
AWS Lambda now supports OAuth authentication for self-managed Apache Kafka event source mappings (ESM), including Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud, Aiven, and Redpanda. With this launch, customers can authenticate their Lambda Kafka consumers through their enterprise identity provider, helping them meet the security and compliance requirements for their Kafka applications.

Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as payment processing, fraud detection, and real-time data pipelines use Kafka ESM to build serverless Kafka consumers. Kafka ESM provides automatic scaling, error handling, batching, and event filtering. Previously, Kafka ESM supported only SASL/PLAIN, SASL/SCRAM, and mutual TLS (mTLS) as authentication methods, so customers in regulated industries that require OAuth could not use Kafka ESM with their clusters. With OAuth support, customers can use their enterprise identity provider, such as Amazon Cognito or Okta, to authenticate their Kafka ESM and apply the same identity governance and access policies across their Kafka clusters and Lambda consumers.

This capability is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To use OAuth authentication, create a new Kafka ESM with your authentication configuration through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS SAM. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda developer guide and AWS Lambda pricing.

title: "When AI Becomes the User: How UI/UX Is Changing in 2026"
description:
When AI Becomes the User: How UI/UX Is Changing in 2026

For years, frontend development and UI/UX design have followed a familiar principle: humans interact with interfaces, and interfaces respond to their actions.

We build buttons for users to click, forms for them to submit, menus for them to navigate, and dashboards for them to analyze data.

A typical user journey looks something like this:

  1. The user opens an application.
  2. They navigate to the required section.
  3. They enter information or apply filters.
  4. They review the results.
  5. They choose an action and confirm it.

This interaction model still works well. But AI is introducing a different way to build and use software.

AI agents can increasingly interpret user goals, use tools, and coordinate multiple steps. Generative UI can also adapt how information and interface components are presented.

Instead of manually operating every part of an application, users can increasingly describe what they want to achieve and let the system help them get there.

This raises an important question for developers: What should we build when users no longer need to interact with every screen themselves?

1. From Traditional UI to Intent-Based Interaction

Consider an e-commerce application.

In a traditional interface, users might need to:

  • Search for a product.
  • Apply price and category filters.
  • Compare several products.
  • Read reviews.
  • Select the best option.

An AI-assisted experience could start with a request:

Find me a reliable laptop under ₹60,000 for web development.

The application could interpret the requirements, retrieve relevant product data, compare specifications, and display a shortlist.

The user still makes the final decision, but the application handles much of the information-gathering process.

This changes the interaction model from action-driven UI to intent-driven UX.

For developers, this doesn't mean removing buttons and forms. It means providing multiple ways to accomplish the same task.

A well-designed application might support both traditional navigation and natural-language requests.

The goal is to reduce unnecessary interaction without sacrificing clarity or control.

2. What Is Generative UI?

Generative UI refers to interfaces that can dynamically produce or assemble UI elements based on a user's request, context, or task.

In a traditional application, developers define the interface structure ahead of time.

For example:

function Dashboard() {
  return (
    <main>
      <h1>Sales Dashboard</h1>
      <SalesChart />
      <RecentOrders />
      <RevenueSummary />
    </main>
  );
}

Every user sees essentially the same predefined components, although the displayed data may differ.

With a generative interface, the application could choose which components to present based on the user's question.

For example:

  • "Show me this month's revenue" could display a revenue chart.
  • "Compare this month with last month" could display a comparison table.
  • "Which products are selling slowly?" could display a filtered product list.

The application doesn't necessarily need to generate arbitrary code. A safer and more predictable approach is to let the AI select from a predefined set of approved UI components.

Conceptually, the model could return structured data such as:

{
  "type": "comparison",
  "title": "Monthly Revenue",
  "metrics": [
    {
      "label": "August",
      "value": 450000
    },
    {
      "label": "September",
      "value": 520000
    }
  ]
}

The frontend then validates this data and renders the appropriate component.

For example:

function renderWidget(widget) {
  switch (widget.type) {
    case "comparison":
      return <ComparisonCard data={widget} />;

    case "chart":
      return <RevenueChart data={widget} />;

    case "table":
      return <DataTable data={widget} />;

    default:
      return <UnsupportedWidget />;
  }
}

This approach keeps the interface flexible while preserving control over the components that can be rendered.

In production, the application should also validate schemas, handle malformed responses, enforce data permissions, and provide accessible fallback states.

3. AI Agents Are Changing Application Workflows

Generative UI changes how interfaces are presented. AI agents introduce another shift: they can help execute multi-step workflows.

Imagine a business owner using an inventory management application.

They ask:

Identify products with low stock and prepare a reorder list.

A traditional application might require the user to open inventory, sort quantities, inspect individual products, and manually prepare a list.

An AI-assisted workflow could:

  1. Retrieve inventory data using authorized tools.
  2. Identify products below a configured stock threshold.
  3. Prepare a reorder list.
  4. Display quantities and relevant product details.
  5. Ask the user to review the list before placing an order.

Notice the distinction between preparing an action and executing it.

The AI may be allowed to analyze inventory automatically, while actually submitting a purchase order could require explicit approval.

This is where backend architecture, permissions, and UX design become closely connected.

An AI agent should not receive unrestricted access to every application operation simply because it can call tools.

Each operation needs appropriate authorization, input validation, and error handling.

4. The Frontend Challenges of AI-Powered Interfaces

Building AI-powered UX introduces several challenges that conventional frontend applications may not encounter in the same way.

Handling Unpredictable Responses

Traditional APIs often return predictable data structures. AI-generated responses may be incomplete, malformed, or inconsistent with the expected schema.

Use schema validation before rendering model-generated UI configurations.

Never assume that an AI response is valid just because it contains JSON.

Managing Loading and Streaming States

AI operations may take longer than ordinary API requests.

Instead of showing a blank screen, provide useful feedback such as:

  • Understanding your request.
  • Retrieving relevant information.
  • Preparing your results.
  • Waiting for your confirmation.

Only display progress stages that accurately reflect the application's actual workflow.

Maintaining Accessibility

Dynamically generated interfaces must still support keyboard navigation, screen readers, appropriate focus management, and semantic HTML.

When a new component appears, users should be able to understand where it fits into the current page and how to interact with it.

Preserving Application State

When an interface changes dynamically, users should not lose their previous inputs, selections, or context.

Developers need to consider how generated components interact with routing, form state, browser navigation, and application-level state management.

Designing for Failure

AI systems can misunderstand requests, retrieve incomplete information, or fail to complete a tool operation.

Provide meaningful error messages, retry options where appropriate, and a clear path back to traditional controls.

A useful AI interface should make failure recoverable rather than forcing users to restart the entire workflow.

5. Trust, Permissions, and Human Control

One of the biggest mistakes in AI product development is assuming that greater automation automatically creates a better user experience.

It doesn't.

Consider three possible actions in a business application:

  • Summarizing sales data.
  • Drafting an email to a customer.
  • Sending that email to hundreds of customers.

These actions carry different levels of risk.

Summarizing data may be a low-risk operation when access permissions are correctly enforced. Drafting an email creates something the user can review. Sending the email has an external consequence and may require explicit confirmation.

The interface should communicate these differences.

A useful design principle is to match the level of AI autonomy to the risk of the action.

For developers, this means implementing:

  • Tool-level authorization.
  • Permission checks on the server.
  • Clear confirmation flows for consequential actions.
  • Audit logs for important operations.
  • Safe handling of failed or partially completed workflows.
  • Options to review or cancel supported actions.

Human control is not an extra feature added after AI integration. It is part of the system design.

6. Does AI Replace Traditional UI Components?

No. Traditional UI components remain essential.

A dashboard is effective for monitoring multiple metrics. A table is useful for comparing structured data. A form is appropriate when users must enter precise information. A confirmation dialog is valuable when an action has significant consequences.

Conversational interfaces are not automatically better than graphical interfaces for every task.

In many applications, the best approach is a hybrid experience:

  • Natural language for expressing goals.
  • AI agents for coordinating multi-step tasks.
  • Charts and tables for understanding results.
  • Forms for structured input.
  • Confirmation screens for important actions.

The challenge is not to replace every interface with a chatbot.

It is to choose the interaction pattern that best supports the task.

7. A Practical Architecture for AI-Driven UI

A maintainable AI-powered application can separate responsibilities into a few clear layers.

User interface: Collects requests, renders approved components, and displays loading, error, and confirmation states.

AI orchestration layer: Interprets requests, determines which authorized tools are needed, and coordinates the workflow.

Application APIs: Retrieve or modify business data through established server-side operations.

Validation and permission layer: Verifies inputs, checks access rights, and ensures that proposed actions comply with application rules.

Human approval layer: Requests confirmation when an operation requires user review.

A simplified workflow looks like this:

User describes a goal
        |
        v
AI interprets the request
        |
        v
Application validates the request
        |
        v
Authorized tools retrieve information
        |
        v
Frontend renders the results
        |
        v
User reviews or confirms an action
        |
        v
Backend executes the approved operation

This is a conceptual architecture rather than a complete implementation. Real systems also need to handle authentication, observability, timeouts, retries, data privacy, and partial failures.

The key idea is to keep AI-generated decisions separate from the trusted application logic that enforces permissions and performs sensitive operations.

8. What Developers Should Focus on in 2026

As AI becomes more integrated into software products, several skills and practices are becoming increasingly useful:

  • Component-driven architecture: Build reusable components that can support different interface layouts.
  • Schema validation: Treat model output as untrusted input.
  • API and tool design: Expose narrowly scoped operations with clear contracts.
  • State management: Preserve user context across dynamic interactions.
  • Accessibility: Ensure AI-generated experiences remain usable by different people.
  • Security: Enforce permissions on the server rather than relying on the frontend or the model.
  • Human-centered UX: Decide when automation helps and when users need control.

These practices are useful even when a product doesn't use generative UI. They help make complex applications more reliable and maintainable.

Final Thoughts

AI is changing UI/UX design beyond automated layouts and conversational interfaces.

It is changing how users express goals, how software executes tasks, and how frontend and backend systems work together.

For developers, the opportunity is not simply to connect a language model to an existing application. It is to rethink how people interact with software while preserving reliability, accessibility, security, and user control.

Generative UI can make interfaces more adaptable. AI agents can simplify complex workflows. But neither removes the need for thoughtful engineering.

The future of UI/UX isn't about building interfaces that users never touch. It's about building software that understands what users need, helps them get there, and keeps them in control.

What do you think: will AI-driven interfaces complement traditional UI, or will they fundamentally change how we build applications?

I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments.

title: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints
description:
Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio now supports custom Tooling blueprints, giving domain administrators the ability to define the foundation of every project by using their own AWS CloudFormation templates. Administrators can tailor project environments to meet organization-specific requirements, such as IAM role names that comply with company naming standards or custom permissions boundaries instead of AWS managed policies.

Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio administrators start by authoring a CloudFormation template that describes the project environment they need, then register it as a custom Tooling blueprint. The service validates the template at registration and again after each project deployment, confirming that the required resources exist before any team member uses the project. Templates can include any CloudFormation-supported resource, such as AWS Lake Formation grants, Amazon Athena workgroups, or VPC security groups, and work across multiple AWS accounts and Regions without per-project edits. At deployment time, the service automatically populates reserved template parameters, such as the project ID and domain ID, so administrators define the template once and apply it everywhere.

This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio is available. To learn more, visit the Custom blueprints as Tooling documentation.
